The Blue Yeti is a household name in microphones for a reason.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've used a Blue Yeti for nearly a decade and it would happily serve for a decade more. A classic design, good hardware controls, and zero fuss. It's not for true audiophiles, but its quality and affordability are still hard to match all these years later.

Key specs: USB A | Four pickup patterns | Hardware gain control

Blue Yeti price check: Best Buy $69.99 | Walmart $69.99

The Blue Yeti might be the most popular USB microphone ever made, and you know what, it earned it. At its usual price, this is a great USB microphone. At $69.99 (its lowest price ever), it's simply one of the best bangs for your buck in this category.

The original Blue Yeti released in 2009, and in 17 years it has barely changed. I've had mine for a decade, and as I look around, I'm realizing it is the longest-lasting gadget on my desk. That's because it just works: I plug in, adjust the gain, and my voice comes through clear.

These days there are more advanced microphones than the Yeti, like its official sequel the Yeti 2, and certainly mics that are just as competitively priced. Those are good too, and I encourage you to check out cheaper options (like the $26 Amazon Basics mic that we surprisingly love) before making any decisions.

But with the Yeti, you absolutely get what it says on the tin. I also think it's still an attractive mic, but it is quite large, so make sure it'll fit on your desk without blocking the corner of your monitor. I've had mine on a mic arm for the past few years, and while it does feel like I'm cosplaying a podcaster just to chill with friends on Discord, it's very convenient.

At this price, it's firmly on the high end of "budget" territory while still sounding as good as mics that cost twice as much. If you do use it for long sessions and prefer to keep your mic open, play with the gain levels and make sure software noise cancelling is on in your chat app of choice (Discord's is pretty good out of the box).

If that's not enough, consider pairing it with dedicated noise cancelling software like Nvidia Broadcast (assuming your GPU can handle the extra toll).

UPDATE: Ubisoft responds, insists staff are not "required" to use AI.

UPDATE 28th NOVEMBER 2026: Ubisoft has provided a statement to press about Vertical Slice's reporting, insisting its staff are not "required" to use Gen AI.

"We encourage our teams to explore where AI can be useful and bring value to their work," the publisher/developer said.

"This doesn't mean that projects are required to use generative AI. Teams need to determine whether, and how, these technologies make sense for the game they want to make and the experience they want to create for players."

ORIGINAL STORY 12th NOVEMBER 2026: Ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process. The French publisher now expects teams pitching new project ideas to be prepared to explain how gen-AI will help with developing the game.Teams who don't want to use gen-AI will need to clearly justify their reasoning to the higher-ups. That's according to a new Vertical Slice report, citing multiple anonymous sources currently working at Ubisoft. Several employees said that pitching a game idea without gen-AI or without explaining why it does not involve the use of the controversial tech will not receive the greenlight. This is especially relevant for smaller games with tight teams who now reportedly must deal with Ubisoft leaders' desire to implement gen-AI if they want to get their pitches reviewed. "We were told that using AI will increase the speed at which pitches can be made by 'small lean agile teams,'" one source said. "We were told that as the goal was to move fast, iterate and discard projects to sift out the good stuff. AI was essential in maintaining a rapid pace." While some said Ubisoft is not openly mandating gen-AI use to staff, others feel "cornered" by gen-AI. One source said Ubisoft views the tech as "unavoidable", and that only a minority of the company's audience reject it. Ubisoft recently gave name to an internal initiative to expand the use of generative-AI and research how its developers can make use of the technology. It's called Motherbrain, and it has its own division within Ubisoft. Over a year ago, Ubisoft embarked on a major restructuring effort that has seen the formation of new subsidiaries, the consolidation of its biggest brands into 'creative houses', the closure of studios and, of course, multiple rounds of layoffs. "Ubisoft is in a top-down nightmare of AI psychosis," one source added, pointing to the already low morale within the company. "Yves [Guillemot] has hitched his wagon to the tech, demanding the rest of the company follow on."

#3624. The PC specs for Mass Effect-like RPG Exodus are basically bearable for a blockbuster space opera in 2026

Not sure how much RAM Matthew McConaughey requires these days

Between Matthew McConaughey, the flesh cathedrals, the space bears, FemJun and the tragedy of Biggs "The Bolt" Keil, the pre-release reveals for Mass Effect-like space RPG Exodus have been a real emotional rollercoaster. It's almost disappointing to learn that the recommended PC system specs are just sort of… fine. Broadly within expectations, by 2026 standards, anyway.

True, you'll need one of those Nvidia RTX 5080 things if you want to play it in 4K at 60fps, but the True Gamer understands that 4K/60FPS is a dangerous and blasphemical overreach, akin to building the Tower of Babel out of cats. 1080p/30FPS was perfectly good enough for Virtua Tennis 3 on Xbox 360, and it'll be perfectly good enough for this game about *squints*… octopus mercenaries. For that, you'll only need an i5-10400, an Nvidia 2060 and a mere 16GB of RAM. Granted, I think new PCs with those components currently cost $200,000, but that isn't Exodus's fault. It's that Jensen Huang who's to blame. Here's the complete spec rundown, anyway.

Will you be playing Exodus? I think it looks swankier so far than Owlcat's surprisingly unconvincing The Expanse: Osiris Reborn, that other great hope of people who mourn Mass Effect 5, but I haven't spent any time with a build. It's out 7th April 2027 - I imagine these recommended specs might alter as they stuff in more McConaughey and layer up the space bears.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock lately, you have probably seen a ton about GTA: VI and how it's set in a fictional version of Florida, and it’s filled with wild characters and kooky situations that only Florida can provide. You don’t have to be a gamer to get a similar experience with Bad Monkey. The show stars Vince Vaughn as a washed-up detective who gets himself wrapped up in some truly oddball cases in Florida.

Apple TV: $6.99 A Month For Black FridaylSign up right now with the Black Friday Deal (Through November 30) to watch Bad Monkey and Slow Horses, plus get all the other hits like Shrinking, Severance, and Ted Lasso, and pay just $6.99 a month for six months. I promise you won'tbe disappointed!

Of course, people love Ted Lasso and Severance, as do I, and those are also available, but for now, for me, my two favs are Bad Monkey and Slow Horses.

#3620. Fed up of Steam's lack of action regarding AI slop? Maybe you should take a look at the 'Games Without AI' event, instead

Yesterday, a new Steam event went live that claims all games featured in it have avoided AI entirely during development. The event, called 'Games Without AI', has been set up by a third party rather than Valve - by Dev Land Marketing, All Ages Of Geek, and Dark Cocooning - to "support real creators" and runs from 25th November to 6th December.

"Behind every game, there are people, ideas, passion, and countless hours of creative work," said a mission statement. "We've carefully curated a selection of independent games that celebrate human creativity, craftsmanship, and collaboration, all made without generative AI. But Games Without AI is more than a festival. It's also about bringing developers, players, and creators together to build a community where we share knowledge, support one another, and grow together."

There are plenty of games featured in the event, and not just ones tied to the organisers, as the cynical-minded amongst you may expect. Ones that jump out to my eye are: Pidgeon Pocket, a 'cozy incremental' with pixel art and a flock of adorable pigeons that you need to upgrade; Bottled by Bears, which tasks you with collecting and discovering rare bees, bottling honey jars, and expanding your farm; and Arctic Awakening, which sort-of looks like Pacific Drive meets Subnautica, in the Arctic.

The event was posted to Reddit where commenters immidiately began accusing certain games of having used AI in their development - often without proof. One user, however, who claims to have been a developer trying to submit a game for inclusion in the event, offered some insight on how the selection process worked.

"As one of participants I can assure you that the qualification process was restrictive[ly] hard to bypass," they wrote. "We were all required to provide proofs of the game being made without AI and share as much of the process as possible. Then it was actually voted by community, which games are convicing enough so the whole process was intended to be as objective as possible. It's an event meant for developers who take pride in their games being made by humans so if any participant attends with ill intend of showing that AI generated game can get through... That would be very sad and shameful. From what I've seen, none of the selected games can be reasonable suspected of that. I also know some other participants personally and they are genuine zero-AI devs."

It's refreshing to see curation turned towards explicitly anti-AI games: between major publishers chasing the trend and smaller indie studios being caught out using the dubious tech, it's nice to see a library of games that promises that no AI was used during development. Given that Valve itself recently claimed it was up to developers themselves to ensure their games couldn't be ripped off by cheap AI tools, I'm happy to see an initiative rallying against the normalcy of all this.

The most recent Steam Next Fest had more than double the number of demos than last year, but that stat isn't what it seems on the surface: roughly 17 percent of those games listed the use of generative AI, but it seemed that many more games did not disclose the use of AI in their development. In June's event, more than a thousand games in Steam Next Fest featured a generative AI disclosure of some kind, which made up roughly 20 percent of all featured games.

Over the past 18 months or so, we've seen the issue of generative AI in games on Steam evolve quite a lot. AI tools have been used to clone games, resulting in a troubling trend of imitation games taking the spotlight away from real indie devs. Whilst Steam, as a storefront, has been steadfast in requiring games to declare their use of generative AI during development, there are loopholes: devs that claim they only use AI tools for "efficiency gains" can appear on the store without any declaration.

At the other end of the spectrum is Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, who last year criticised Valve's requirement to disclose generative AI, saying, "Steam and all digital marketplaces need to drop the 'Made with AI' label. It doesn't matter any more." The swell of users rejecting AI in games, though, seems to run counter to that argument. Recently, Big Walk developer House House revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" during the development of the co-op darling, and received a lot of backlash online.

#3618. The Botanist and the Translator is a planet-wide plant mystery puzzle game published by Team Cherry and made by Hollow Knight: Silksong's own Hornet

It's been a little over a year since Hollow Knight: Silksong launched after an eon of comments on Nintendo Directs asking "SILKSONG???", and now yesterday brought us the news that its first expansion, Sea of Sorrow, is due out next month. And it's free? Well ain't that lovely! Truth be told, however, I was actually a little more interested in everything that preceded the Sea of Sorrow trailer in yesterday's Cherry Time presentation. Namely, The Botanist and the Translator, a ridiculously delightful looking, hand-drawn game about solving a plant related mystery across an alien planet that is being developed by Makoto Koji, the voice actor behind Silksong's Hornet.

In The Botanist and the Translator, you play as Hatti, the titular botanist, alongside Oliver, her equally titular translator who is also a lightly Very Hungry Caterpillar-esque bug. They've been brought to a planet that's been covered in a "thick, sticky pollen," and it's up to them to figure out why all the plants are behaving so strangely. On the one side, as Hatti, you'll be sketching all the various flora you come across, as well as trying to figure out how they all work in point-and-click style puzzle minigames.

On the other side, with Oliver, you speak to all the numerous strange and charming critters across this planet, translating them for Hatti in a simple enough looking rhythm game that mixes things up depending on who's being spoken to. The visual identity on display here is really engrossing, in a short behind the scenes video shared by Team Cherry, Koji speaks of her origins as a children's book illustrator and you can really feel that here. You can get a sense of Team Cherry's influence in the gibberish voice acting too, it's very sweet!

Team Cherry are also publishing The Botanist and the Translator too, an initiative I'm glad to see they're taking given just how loaded they already were and surely once again are following the release of Silksong. There's no release date attached to this one just yet, so all we can do is hope that it doesn't take a Silksong amount of time. And in the meanwhile, we could always throw it a little wishlist on Steam.

If you’re wondering what Tucker Carlson thinks of breakout SNL star Jeremy Culhane’s buzzy impression, the unfortunate truth is we may never know. The popular talking head has apparently never seen it, and it’s not because he’s angry about it or opposed on principle, it’s because he’s against consuming any articles or videos about himself.

Fans love to joke about celebrities setting Google alerts for themselves, but if Carlson is to be believed, he tries to avoid any opinions about himself that don’t come directly from people he knows. He’ll listen to his family. He’ll listen to his friends and those working on his show. He wants their feedback, but when it comes to everyone else, he’d rather just tune out all the noise. Here’s what he told Brandon Straka during their interview...

I don’t watch anything or read anything about myself ever. That is my rule… Focusing on yourself too much is the road to unhappiness.

If that quote did something to you, it’s probably because Tucker uses one of the Tucker-isms Culhane uses all the time in his impression. It feels like every SNL appearance includes at least a couple usages of, “That’s the rule.” It warmed my heart to see it here, and it made me even more impressed with Culhane’s impression, given it almost felt in character the way Carlson said it. Seriously, first check out the interview with Carlson in real life…

I love how Straka basically has a panic attack the second he says, “That’s my rule.” In that moment, he’s all of us freaking out because he just said the thing. If you listen closely to the rest of Tucker’s comments, however, you can hear a lot more of where Culhane’s impression comes from. There’s the cadence in how he speaks, and of course there’s the signature laugh that Carlson has been known for throughout his career.

After his initial comments about never having seen the impression, Carlson went on to talk more generally about being parodied, and he had some really thoughtful things to say about his place in the world and what it’s like to get older. He said when he was a kid, he would look at older people and wonder if they were doing a bit, but as he’s aged and gotten feedback from his kids, he’s slowly realized that everyone sort of becomes a caricature of themselves.

He said he tries not to wear a mask, but sometimes he wonders if everyone eventually grows into one of the facets of their personality. Here’s a portion of his quote…

I do think we all become parodies of ourselves. I remember thinking that of older people when I was younger. I was like, ‘Are you serious? Are you acting? Is this like a bit?’ Maybe it was a bit 30 years ago, but now it’s who you actually are. Your face sorta grew into the mask you wore.

It sounds like Carlson is never going to watch Culhane’s impression, but I would love to see a reaction video of him checking it out for the first time, especially since he has more free reign outside Fox News. I wonder what would be going through his head, especially since it feels like a slightly exaggerated but also pretty realistic take on him as a talking head. It's hard to tell because celebrities have a wide range of opinions about getting parodied on the show. Elon Musk, as an example, doesn't like Culhane's take on him.

Regardless, I’m sure we’ll see Culhane’s impression quite a few more times on Saturday Night Live. It’s become a semi-consistent part of Weekend Update, and it gets tremendous feedback every time. Maybe we’ll even see it return when the show comes back with guest host Amanda Seyfried next weekend.

#3615. After playing the game, 30% of polled GTA 6 players want to buy flowers for a loved one, 9% accidentally punched cats

A new survey of Grand Theft Auto 6 players has found some particularly interesting results. 30 percent came away from the game with the desire to buy someone special flowers. Nine percent punched cats.

Per Games User Research's director Steve Bromley, 303 players from across the UK and US were polled on their experiences. They had to have at least two hours of playtime to contribute, which led to an informed sample of how folks are finding the game.

Those polled gave the game an 8.4/10 (that's 4.2/5 Eurogamer readers), which is glowing praise. 42 percent loved the narrative, as well as Jason and Lucia's relationship. 38 dug the lifelike and believable world, while 35 percent were keen on the freedom to explore and the variety of activities.

As for what they didn't like, 28 percent weren't a fan of the slow pacing and long cutscenes, 19 percent didn't like the difficulty in stealing cars and losing a wanted level, while 18 percent were put off by the game's technical performance.

Now for some fun findings: 41 percent expressed an interest in improving their real life after playing the game, with 30 percent of those looking to buy a loved one some flowers. Nice! 14 percent were at least once confused or stuck, due to confusion with the stealth, identifying time-sensitive missions, or experiencing control issues.

There's some bad news for the cats out there, too. Nine percent accidentally punched a cat while trying to pet it, while 61 percent had the same experience with human NPCs. At least it wasn't intentional, that has to count for something. Right?

#3614. Warframe is ready to welcome you to its second solar system, as its big free Tau update gets an early December release date

Warframe continues to be a game that whenever I hear it's getting a new anything I just think, "wow, that thing's still going!" Not in a "why would anyone play this" kind of way, in a just simply being pleased to see an occasionally striking game retain and even successfully grow an audience in this age where everything else is dying a horrific death way. And today I am once again thinking, "wow, that thing's still going," as a release date has been confirmed for Tau, a massive, free new update that brings a second solar system to the sci-fi shooter.

As previously noted by Edwin, Tau is coated in a noir theming that feels a touch novel given its maximalist sci-fi vibes. There's a lot to be found on Tau in this update, namely a new city called Fornax, the game's "first interconnected social hub system full of various characters and vendors to meet," as noted in a press release. There are three different hubs you can move between either by foot or car, and new game modes to try out such as Racket, "where squads must recover stolen funds and deliver them to extorted neighborhoods, or Mayhem, and disrupt unsavory operations of the mob by literally causing destruction and mayhem."

Given the noir vibes, there is of course some kind of mystery to be solved, with clues to collect and suspects to interrogate across three sub-factions, Larynde's Dazzlers, The Haulers, "and a yet-to-be-revealed group, leading to a climactic conclusion." You do all this as The Fornax Informer, which I think is just the sci-fi version of a gumshoe. Please don't ask me for certainty on this, I cannot stress how not embedded in the Warframe space I am any harder.

Either way, sounds like it's a big update! There's of course cosmetic to pick up too, and access to Kullervo Prime will drop the same day. I'm sure there'll be even more to discover on the day, which is, drumroll please… December 9th! Not too long of a wait now is it? Ignoring the presumable years some of you have been waiting for such an update, that is. Anyway, happy Warframing!

Exclusive: Assassin's Creed director Stefan Schwartz gives an update on the Netflix series

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix's upcoming Assassin's Creed show will be true to the games, its director has promised. Stefan Schwartz, who directed several episodes of the upcoming series, shared an update on its progress with GamesRadar+.

The series is set in the world of the franchise but tells an original story, according to the streaming service. However, as Schwartz points out: "It's very much in the lore of Assassin's Creed, it's still very much in it, and I think it's a fun version of that world: big scale and lots of running on roofs."

The show wrapped filming in November 2026 after filming on location. "Yes, that was hot and lovely," Schwartz smiles when asked about filming in Rome. "[It was] also shot a little bit in Bulgaria as well. So I'm still editing that now."

Set in 64AD, exact story details for the upcoming live-action show are being kept under wraps, but according to Netflix it will tell an "original story set in the heart of the Roman Empire".

Furious star Lola Petticrew stars in the series alongside Toby Wallace, Zachary Hart, and Laura Marcus. Noomi Rapace, Ramzy Bedia, and Sean Harris are also set to star in recurring roles.

GamesRadar+ was speaking to Schwartz following his work directing The Rings of Power season 3 episode 7, which features the crafting of the One Ring for the first time on screen. He opened up about the "huge pressure" of adapting the moment without much in Tolkien's work to go off.

The Rings of Power season 3 is available to watch now on Prime Video. The Assassin's Creed show is coming to Netflix at some point.

#3611. "EA's always wanted everything to be a live service": BioWare vet Mark Darrah on EA treating the Mass Effect dev as "just an afterthought"

That feeling certainly still seems to be the case

BioWare are obviously predominantly known and loved for their single-player RPG output, given that that's where their origins lie and they found their greatest strengths amongst the likes of Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Of course, they've also worked on some big series like Star Wars, and it's for that reason, and the fact they were specifically working on a Star Wars MMO, that BioWare vet Mark Darrah thinks EA decided to acquire the studio.

Speaking to Pembridge TV (ta, GamesRadar), Darrah explain that "EA's always wanted everything to be a live service. They just didn't use that language in the past. Back in the days before Destiny, the thing that was seen as the successful live service model was the MMO. Everyone wanted an MMO. World of Warcraft came out and totally redefined the space. Everyone wanted a World of Warcraft killer. I mean, it was Star Wars. Surely it could be the World of Warcraft killer."

That World of Warcraft killer was meant to be Star Wars: The Old Republic, an MMO follow-up to the singleplayer Knights of the Old Republic. You can see why a mind poisoned by graphs and charts and business would find this appealing. The problem was that The Old Republic was being made by the newer BioWare Austin, whereas the singleplayer releases were being continued at the original Edmonton studio. And thusly, EA bought the whole lot of them, alongside Pandemic who at the time were making Star Wars: Battlefront, leaving the Edmonton studio a bit in the lurch.

"It's like, 'okay, well, they really want Star Wars: The Old Republic. They want the MMO. They obviously want [Battlefront],'" Darrah said. "Then it's like, 'oh, and they're getting BioWare Edmonton.' For me, and for many people in Edmonton at the time of the acquisition, it looked like EA was buying Star Wars: The Old Republic and Pandemic and getting BioWare Edmonton as a side effect."

Ultimately The Old Republic wasn't as popular as EA wanted it to be. "EA hated SWTOR from the beginning," Darrah explained. "They wanted it really bad, but all indication - and someone from Austin could probably speak to this more than me - it always seemed to me like they wanted it gone pretty much from the instant it launched and didn't hit its numbers. They never wanted to invest in it. They always wanted to push it out of the conversation. They talked about pulling people off of it for a really long time. But it did generate money."

Darrah did note that The Old Republic eventually "more than paid for itself," it's just that it took a while. "The probably single best return on investment that EA got was BioWare Edmonton, even though it seemed like we were just an afterthought." Obviously, unfortunately, after years of continuing that fruitless live service endeavour, forcing BioWare into making types of games they aren't known for, the studio has now been shut down, with the latest (lightly leaked) Mass Effect no longer in development. And once again, it all just seems to come back to Star Wars for EA. Continued solidarity with all those affected by BioWare closure.

It’s been 16 years since the last time we hung out with Greg Focker and his in-laws, and it’s been 26 years since he met the parents. However, the various bits from those original Meet the Parents movies have stuck with me. So, I was thrilled to see so many A+ references to them in Focker In-Law. However, there was one callback in this project on the 2026 movie schedule that was very extreme.

As was to be expected when Ariana Grande joined Focker In-Law as the newest potential in-law, hijinks and lie detector tests were going to happen. Plus, with Ben Stiller’s Greg now in the position Robert De Niro’s Jack was in during the first movie, the script was flipped, which provided a fun foundation to return to some very funny gags.

First of all, I thought the way they brought the lie detector back into this movie was delightful. Watching Olivia be tested was really funny, and knowing that Greg had to go through a much tougher version of that in Meet the Parents made the whole situation even better.

Getting into a specific Easter egg, I wasn’t expecting the Gaylord callbacks in this movie at all. As you might remember, Greg Focker’s legal name is Gaylord Focker. And in Focker In-Law, that comes up because his daughter, Samantha (Beanie Feldstein), will use it every now and again. I loved how casual the reference was, and I couldn't help but chuckle at the "if you know, you know" nature of this whole ongoing joke.

Of course, there were many other A+ Easter eggs and jokes that called back to the earlier movies – like everything having to do with the Circle of Trust and Owen Wilson’s character, Kevin. However, the one I really can’t get over has to do with Jinx the cat.

I expected some wild things to happen in Focker In-Law. To this day, I remember the shock I felt over the absolutely crazy situations that happened in Meet the Parents and Meet the Fockers (which you can stream with a Peacock subscription). However, I did not expect Jinx the cat to be taxidermied. I did not expect Jack’s dog, Lazarus, to have beef with the late cat. And I certainly did not expect the German shepherd to eat the taxidermied Jinx in the movie.

Really, any moment involving the iconic cat made me crack up. I couldn’t get over the fact that they paid homage to him by having him taxidermied.

However, it was when Jinx got involved in a battle between Greg and Lazarus that I couldn’t keep it together. In an effort to get the dog off his back, Greg grabbed the cat and threw it. The dog went after it and ripped it to shreds.

My jaw was legitimately on the floor when this happened, and I was laughing so hard I was crying. Honestly, I couldn’t believe they went there with Jinxie. I mean, that cat was Jack's pride and joy, and now he's been ripped to shreds. However, it added to the glorious absurdity of this film.

Now, if you’d like to see this wild moment for yourself, you can catch Focker In-Law in theaters now.

Riley Utley is the Weekend Editor at CinemaBlend. Since joining the CB team she has covered numerous TV shows and movies -- including her personal favorite shows Ted Lasso and The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel. She also has followed and consistently written about everything from Taylor Swift to Fire Country, and she's enjoyed every second of it.

#3609. We are already in a world where people think about promoting games as human-made, Citizen Sleeper creator says

Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - believes we're reaching a point of gen-AI saturation whereby game-makers are starting to counter-promote games as being human-made.

"We already are. Yeah, yeah, yeah. 100 percent," Damian Martin told me in an interview, while discussing their striking new game Signet City. "That was already something that my publisher [Fellow Traveller] was saying they want to do with my games more, especially with me doing the art this time as well. Yeah, 100 percent - it's going to give rise to that."

It's a label I haven't seen circulating in games yet, but we have seen an increase in the number of AI disclosures for games being sold on Steam, and many videos on YouTube now carry 'No AI' badges, in an effort to stand out from the torrent of videos made using gen-AI. We are already seeing Steam events dedicated to games without any AI usage whatsoever. Things are clearly changing.

Damian Martin told me "the only good thing" that could come from gen-AI use is a bounce-back effect of people noticing and cherishing human-made things more. They were reminded of this while looking at a Rembrandt sketch while doing a brief stint in art school ahead of Signet City (the art in the Citizen Sleeper games was commissioned, but the art in Signet City is done by them). In the sketch, the faces had been scribbled out, presumably because Rembrandt didn't like the work he'd done. They were scribbles that revealed the humanity of the creator.

"You suddenly remember that trying to represent a human face by using a pencil and a piece of paper is something that's been happening for hundreds of years," Damian Martin said. "So when you do it, you're connecting to an entire history of that challenge and that opportunity, and it's fascinating to me to engage and be part of that. It's really beautiful.

"If AI makes us notice that more," they added, "then I think that's great. If we can make a counter-punch, if we can find that energy, that's great. I certainly think if it gives value to human-made things, in a way that perhaps we'd been forgetting, then that's the only good thing that can come from that process."

To be clear, Damian Martin is not using gen-AI in making Signet City, a game about being a parasite in people's heads in a fictional version of Newcastle in the 1980s and then influencing what they do. It's a game with a distinct hand-drawn look, presented in a thick-lined, moody black-and-white way, and with bleak industrial backgrounds and post-punk influences and energy. Indeed, the idea Damian Martin would use gen-AI in any way runs counter and contrary to what they're known for.

"I exist in this space where the idea that I would use AI is kind of mad," they said. "It's a bit like me saying, 'I'm going to start buying all of my art materials from the asset store on Unity.' The reason people buy my games is because they come from me, and the only evidence I have - the only thing I can trust - is my own expression and identity. That's the thing that's worked for me; there's no other judgeable thing. So I'm working to put more of that into my games.

"But there is a real threat," they added, "and the reason there is a real threat in the wider games industry is because it's an industry, and people who work on games for big companies, in my experience, are treated very poorly. They are not respected as human beings in a lot of cases. So why would they not be replaced by machines if the people who pay their wages do not even respect their human nature? They do not respect their creativity. We've seen such a lack of respect for expression, for directors, for individuals within games."

"When something is industrial production and it doesn't care about the people involved, then it doesn't care whether they're machines or they're people as long as the work happens, and that's the real threat," they reiterated. "So we do have to be vigilant, and we do have to be loud and say stuff, and say that it's not okay for us, because otherwise it will happen. It just seems inevitable that you would try to automate these things because it's easier than having employees; that's the kind of horrible logic of industry, unfortunately. But that doesn't really concern me because I'm operating in a completely different mode."

Signet City currently has no release date but was said to be halfway through development when announced this summer. Citizen Sleeper 2 - Damian Martin's most recent game - was released at the beginning of 2025. It's a sequel that introduced more pressure into the heartwarming sci-fi, dice-rolling, role-playing series, and I thought it better for it. "With a new found sense of tension, and showpiece Contract missions, Citizen Sleeper is transformed. This follow-up has improved the RPG formula in every way," I wrote in my Citizen Sleeper 2 review.

#3608. Rockstar Games employees vote against union recognition

Rockstar Games employees have voted against official recognition of the Rockstar Game Workers Union, with 93.2 percent of staff participating in the vote.

25 percent of those who participated voted to recognise the union, while 75 percent voted against. If it had been approved, it would have been the largest recognised union in the UK video game industry by a large margin. While the union will still exist and organise, Rockstar Games will not have to recognise the union as a representing body for staff at the studio, and is not obligated to attend regular meetings with the body.

Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar Games told Eurogamer: "We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we've built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. This result reflects our team's strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we're excited to build on all we've accomplished together."

The Rockstar Union also released a statement following the outcome of this vote, saying Rockstar employees will continue to organise despite the lack of recognition. It reads:

"For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn't a sign to retreat, it's a sign to double down on what we stand for. Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We're ready to put in the effort to make that happen.

"Whilst we haven't emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening. People entirely unfamiliar with unions were for the first time debating employment conditions, collective bargaining rights, and our contracts. We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions can lead us.

"A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it's one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We'll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against Al and layoffs.

"The power to shape our working lives has always been, and will always be, in our hands."

Rockstar employees represented by the union are still awaiting the verdict from the Rockstar Games vs IWGB employment tribunal legal case, of which the final verdict is still pending. This case was kicked off by the sudden firing of employees present in a union Discord server. The employees claim this was an attempt at union busting by Rockstar, while the company denies this, saying it was for breaking confidentiality agreements.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before id Software created its excellent 2016 reboot of Doom, the studio was working on a more direct follow-up to its earlier demon-blasters. Doom 4 was in production between 2008 and 2011, and much like Doom 3, followed popular trends of first-person shooters at the time. But after multiple false-starts, id Software went back to the drawing board, resulting in the glory-killing FPS that has defined the series' direction ever since.

But according to one former id Software developer, Doom 4 was by no means a terrible game, and possibly should have even been released in some form. It just had one big problem—it wasn't Doom.

Speaking to FRVR, former id Software principal programmer Dustin Land said that he thought Doom 4 showed a lot of promise. "I never thought there was anything wrong with that game", he explained. Unlike the 2016 reboot, Doom 4 aimed to be more of a narrative and spectacle-driven experience, channeling the approach of concurrent shooters like Call of Duty. "Playing Call of Duty but you're shooting demons is actually a fun game," Land continued. "The problem is always that it's not Doom. And so the question is always 'What's Doom'?"

Yet while Doom 4 may not have been a fit for the series, Land believes that Doom 4 could have stood up on its own merits. "I thought it could've just been a new IP. It could've been sold under some other brand."

Obviously, this didn't happen. After three years of trying, Doom 4 was canned, and afterward id Software spent a good while figuring out what the next Doom should look like. "It was a laborious process," Land says. "It was a couple years trying to find what exactly it should be. And that was the era of cover-based shooters, long-distance poking, health recovery, stuff like that. And so the push-forward combat really subverted people's expectation of what a first-person [shooter] should be, and it's had a large impact on how shooters are designed these days."

This is certainly true for id's own lineage, with every subsequent Doom game since 2016 looking to reinvent how the Doom Slayer fights. What lies in store for id Software next remains unclear, however. While the studio is purportedly working on a new project, in the summer, Xbox laid off a reported 136 developers from id Software. Earlier this month, Land announced the formation of Hidden Horses, a new, democratically governed studio composed of former id Software developers, which is working on a new shooter based on The Running Man and 1990's Smash TV.

Head back to 2021 to read our epic cover feature on Dune, featuring interviews with the cast and director Denis Villeneuve

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ahead of the release of the final film in Denis Villeneuve's Dune trilogy, we're heading back to where it all began. In this 2021 feature we went deep with the cast and creators of the first movie, unpicking the legacy of the previous Dune adaptation as Villeneuve told us in his own words what he wanted his new vision of this world to be.

Taken from issue 315 of Total Film, this feature has interviews from the director as well as his cast, including Timothée Chalamet, Rebecca Ferguson, Oscar Isaac, Josh Brolin, Zendaya, and Jason Momoa, for the ultimate preview. So strap in and travel back in time with us to Arrakis to celebrate our first entry into the incredible universe that this first movie established on screen.

There's no doubt that Dune 3 is one of the biggest upcoming movies of the year, due to hit theaters the same day as Avengers: Doomsday. Based on everything we've seen so far, it looks set to be an epic conclusion to one of the best adaptations to grace our screens. So when you're done reading this time capsule report, why not keep revisiting the previous movies with our interview with Villeneuve when Dune 2 became our 2024 film of the year.

Denis Villeneuve was barely a teenager when he first dreamed of a scorching desert planet in a galaxy far, far away, but probably not the one you're thinking of. He dreamed of Arrakis. Of colossal sandworms, roaming a parched landscape loaded with mystery. Of miraculous stillsuits and psychotropic spice. Of powerful families locked in a life or death struggle, and the indigenous, blue-eyed freedom fighters whose lands they exploit. He dreamed of Paul Atreides, a young man not much older than himself who was destined to lead armies. He dreamed of Dune.

"I'm still deeply moved to have had the chance to tackle this dream, to play with this dream, to go back to this dream," an impassioned Villeneuve tells Total Film over Zoom in late June, roughly three months after finishing work on Part One of a proposed two-part adaptation. Reading Dune as a 14-year-old while growing up in Quebec proved a foundational experience for a filmmaker who is fast proving himself without equal.

He considered Herbert's philosophical, spiritual, ecologically conscious novel about a young man coming of age in the most testing circumstances "almost a guide to life". With his closest friend, he would draw his hero Paul riding sandworms – illustrations he's kept safe to this day. Dune wasn't just formative for Villeneuve, it's his Rosetta Stone.

"Denis said to me [Paul Atreides] was the character he saw his sort of tortured adolescence through, and a figure for him to escape through," says Timothée Chalamet, who has just wrapped Bones & All, his reunion with Call Me By Your Name's Luca Guadagnino, when he hops on Zoom with TF. The pressure of literally embodying Villeneuve's dreams was not lost on the 25-year-old actor – the filmmaker's first and only choice for the role – but no one felt that pressure more than Villeneuve himself.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"It was," the director stresses, "by far, the toughest thing I've done. There are deep pleasures when there are images that you're able to achieve that are close to what you had in mind as a teenager; then it's orgasmic. But the failures are very difficult, because you disappoint the teenager in yourself. As Hans Zimmer pointed out, it's very dangerous to try to reach one of your oldest dreams."

The very idea of adapting Dune was an "inaccessible, out-of-reach dream" that Villeneuve carried throughout his career as a filmmaker. One of his earliest feature films, 2010's acclaimed drama Incendies, was shot in the deserts of Wadi Rum, Jordan, the very same alien landscapes he would return to almost a decade later for Dune. "I remember taking mental notes at the time: 'If ever I do the movie, I'm coming back here and there. That's where Paul sits...'" he recalls. "But it was a massive fantasy."

Villeneuve is the first to admit that he could not have done Dune justice a decade ago. Only by making stepping stone movies Arrival – where he learnt to tell interior stories on a large canvas – and Blade Runner 2049 – a crash-course in futuristic world building – did he feel equipped to bring a book of Dune's scale and complexity, one long considered unadaptable, to the screen. "I have some kind of a self destructive device inside me to take projects that are out of my reach," he acknowledges. But in those moments of uncertainty he would turn to a mantra from a book that shaped his adolescence: "I must not fear. Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration. I will face my fear."

"I'm still deeply moved to have had the chance to tackle this dream, to play with this dream, to go back to this dream."

Fear and excitement collided in November 2016 when production company Legendary acquired the screen rights to Frank Herbert's far-future saga. Just a month later, following "the shortest meeting of my career", Villeneuve had signed on to direct his dream project. A crucial early decision was that Herbert's 400-plus-page opus would need to be told across two films, lest this new adaptation suffer the same fate as David Lynch's failed '84 film, which jettisoned much of the novel’s second half for the sake of a commercially friendly runtime. "David Lynch is a master. He truly is one of the greatest filmmakers of the past 50 years," says Villeneuve. "When I saw his adaptation, there were things in it that I loved, but I thought there was still something that could be made closer to the spirit of the book."

The challenge in adapting Dune, at least on paper, isn't its scale (though did we mention the giant freakin' sandworms?); conversely it's the intimacy, and Herbert's poetic prose, which digs deep into the interior lives of its expansive cast of characters. As Villeneuve notes, "the book is very theatrical" with scenes mostly consisting of characters standing around rooms talking – hardly the domain of tentpole film fare. "We had to find ways to bring it more towards cinema. It was not easy to do," he acknowledges. That meant no voiceover, a device the Lynch adaptation proved the pitfalls of, while splitting the book in two required every major structural decision across both films be locked from the outset, but it was never as simple as cutting the book in half.

"There were certain broad-stroke decisions that were made, just to find the most dynamic way to tell the story. We had to shovel some things into Part Two for the mental sanity of everybody," Villeneuve says, pointing to feared Harkonnen fighter Feyd Rautha, previously played by Sting in cinema's most flamboyant underpants ("It was the most powerful image, that jockstrap," muses Villeneuve), as a character who appears early in the novel, but not in Dune: Part One.

"The book is so rich," says Villeneuve. "There are so many fantastic details about the different cultures. In order to preserve and have the time to bring that to the screen, we had to make important choices."

Both Legendary and distributor Warner Bros embraced the idea of a two-part Dune adaptation "right at the start". Villeneuve even hoped to shoot both movies simultaneously "but it was too expensive, too big, and I think the studio wanted to see what would happen with the first one before we start to move forward."

The decision ultimately proved a blessing. "Because I would be dead right now! I don’t know how Peter Jackson did it," he concedes. "We were working in extreme conditions – in the storms, high winds, high heat. So it's good to recharge, to regroup, to dream a bit more, to bring something new to Dune: Part Two."

Before Villeneuve can return to Arrakis, audiences still have to take their maiden voyage across the stars. Set thousands of years in the future, Dune is the story of Paul Atreides, heir apparent to his father Duke Leto Atreides (Oscar Isaac) and mother Lady Jessica (Rebecca Ferguson) on their home planet of Caladan. Under orders of the Emperor, House Atreides is assigned fiefdom over Arrakis. Also known as Dune, the desert planet is the universe's sole source of the spice melange, a valuable, mind-altering narcotic that, among other things, makes warp space navigation possible.

"Working with great directors is the biggest priority for me. To have a director like Denis, who’s in the prime of his career, working on a project of this size, in addition to the source material being so influential, and then the role within that of Paul Atreides being something so fun to wrestle with – this great, terrible purpose that he feels – it all made Dune the most desirable project to work on."

The outgoing Harkonnens, led by the monstrous Baron (Stellan Skarsgård), have no intention of accepting their expulsion from Arrakis peacefully, while the native Fremen, who live in harmony with the desert, fight for the preservation of their people and planet, including the immense sandworms, which devour anyone foolish enough to attract their attention.

All this happens at a crucial time for Paul. Every night he dreams – or are they visions? – of a young Fremen woman, Chani (Zendaya), while the mystical Bene Gesserit sisterhood believe Paul could be the messianic Kwiswatz Haderach – a being with powerful prescient abilities that they've been working towards the arrival of for millenia.

"It was really a movie inspired by Timothée [Chalamet]," says Villeneuve, who co-wrote Dune with the actor in mind months before he officially signed on. "Paul Atreides is a rock star. You need someone that will lead a whole planet, literally. You need someone that has tremendous charisma."

In the novel, Paul is just 16 years old. Chalamet was 23 at the time of filming, though Villeneuve and director of photography Greig Fraser were frequently struck by how young he looked through the lens. More important was that Chalamet convey Paul's precocious wisdom and capacity to adapt. "He has a seriously old soul," Villeneuve says. "He's someone that is very, very thoughtful and intellectual, and he's an insane actor. He brought that turmoil, that hurricane inside Paul Atreides."

Chalamet had been keeping tabs on the production from the moment it was announced, and would fortuitously find himself at many of the same events as Villeneuve over the course of 2017, as the pair did the publicity rounds for Blade Runner 2049 and Call Me By Your Name. "I would always try to put myself in front of him, and just say 'Hi', and not be annoying or burdensome," a modest Chalamet remembers. "I just tried to put myself on his radar, because I knew what a great part Paul Atreides was." After circling each other for months, Villeneuve invited Chalamet to meet him in Cannes, where he was serving on the Festival jury. The pair agreed to work together on the spot.

From there, Villeneuve built the cast around Chalamet, recruiting choice collaborators from previous films, including Sicario's Josh Brolin as Paul's mentor and war master Gurney Halleck, Blade Runner 2049's Dave Bautista as the barbaric 'Beast' Rabban Harkonnen, and Prisoners' David Dastmalchian as the twisted Harkonnen mentat (a sort of human computer, it's a whole thing) Piter De Vries.

But the wildly star-studded cast was largely new to the filmmaker. In addition to Isaac, Ferguson, Zendaya and Skarsgård, Aquaman star Jason Momoa jumped at the chance to play greatest fighter in the galaxy Duncan Idaho, Javier Bardem leads the Fremen as man of few words Stilgar, Charlotte Rampling wields the deadly Gom Jabbar as Reverend Mother Gaius Helen Mohaim, while Sharon Duncan Brewster stars as gender-swapped Arrakis ecologist Dr. Liet Kynes.

"It was really a movie inspired by Timothée [Chalamet]. Paul Atreides is a rock star."

The cast paint a picture of Villeneuve as director with an unwaveringly clear vision for Dune, but one refreshingly open to collaboration. Like Paul Atreides, whose subconscious thoughts reveal visions of possible futures, Villeneuve was often guided by images that came in his sleep – an opportunity, perhaps, to reconnect with the teenage dreamer inside.

"He'll call me at like three o'clock in the morning," Brolin explains, "And he'll go [adopts French accent] 'Listen, my friend, I had a dream last night. I need to talk to you. I don't think this scene works. I think we need to…' So he relies a lot on his imagination." A common sentiment among the cast is that Villeneuve could sell sand at the beach, according to Ferguson, thanks to his infectious passion for Herbert's world. "It was a bible for him, since he was young. And I got to be on the receiving end of him explaining his love. He could have given me any role, and I would do it."

Another key appeal for the cast – many well-versed in blockbuster filmmaking – was the insistence on shooting as much of the film as feasibly possible for real, with towering sets constructed at Origo Studios in Budapest, while Wadi Rum in Jordan and Abu Dhabi doubled for Dune's vast desert expanse. Reuniting with production designer Patrice Vermette, a regular collaborator going back to Prisoners, the pair agreed that "Paul needed to be put in an environment that was of a massive scale; a scale that he has never experienced," Vermette says. "So it's totally overwhelming."

For the Atreides' rugged home on Caladan (filmed in Norway), Vermette was inspired by his trips to the Canadian coast, symbolising "the death of an old world, but also the birth of something new". The massive city of Arrakeen, the seat of power on Arrakis, has at its pinnacle a ziggurat megastructure where the Atreides take up residence. Inspired by Soviet-era bunker architecture, Vermette constructed immense, 25ft tall chambers, with even larger sets – including the enormous Arrakeen staircase – assembled on an exterior backlot. "The sets that were built were just massive. They're unreal," adds Momoa. "It was pretty easy to be an actor, to be in that world."

Numerous full-scale ornithopters – Dune's dragonfly-like choppers – were built and could do everything Herbert imagined, short of taking off. Chalamet spent two weeks ahead of filming getting accustomed to the ornithopter cockpit, so that each flipped switch and button press could be accomplished with conviction on screen. For Villeneuve, the scale was vital in order to capture "that strong feeling of loneliness and isolation that one can feel on Arrakis". He would often think back to his time a decade earlier making Incendies, and how even Herbert's prose couldn't fully capture the desert's majesty. "The deeper you go into the desert, the closer you get to your inner self," Villeneuve considers. "It's like an inner journey. The infinity is a mirror of your own psyche. There's something about that that always amazed me."

Visual effects were a crucial element, of course. Without VFX house DNEG, who won the Oscar for Blade Runner 2049 back in 2018, there would be no sandworms, no twin moons dominating the Arrakis sky and significantly fewer fireworks when the spice hits the fan. But most of the cast attest to never seeing a single green or blue screen throughout the four-month shoot, and when set extensions were required Vermette and Fraser would instead use fabric screens dyed to the set's average colour so that the quality of light would never be compromised. "We scratched our head a lot, because we really wanted to give Denis and the actors immersive environments," Vermette says. "We stretched our limits."

"This whole thing has been a magical experience. I've always kind of been a huge fan of sci-fi. I've always wanted to be a part of something that It feels like, quite literally, another world. Just being there, it was incredible. I was blown away by the entire experience and being able to work with Denis and Timothée and everybody. It blew my mind, and I just felt so lucky to be there, and be immersed in this. It really did feel like just being in a completely different world."

Bringing Arrakis to life convincingly was all-important because, as Villeneuve points out, "it’s probably the main character in Dune" – a cliché, but one that holds true. Counter-intuitively for a film set millennia from now, in a far off galaxy, Villeneuve resisted anything that felt too otherworldly. "I didn’t want to create an alien landscape that is so exotic, that you feel disconnected," he explains. "It should feel tactile, that you could be there on the planet. We needed to kill the exoticism, in a strange way."

That thinking extended to every aspect of the production, including the costume department, where co-costume designers Jacqueline West and Bob Morgan labelled the film's hybrid style "modieval" – more War of the Roses than Star Wars. Steering clear of genre inspirations, the pair undertook unconventional research. The black dresses of the Bene Gesserit sisterhood, for example, were drawn from tarot cards; the chunky Atreides battle armor was modelled on medieval suits of armor; the Sardukar – the Emperor's elite mercenaries – mirrored the SS; while the Fremen "were really my French Resistance," says West. On some days, the costume department had to outfit four actual armies. "It was by far the biggest costume project I've ever done," West says.

No costume is more important to Dune, however, than the stillsuit. Worn primarily by the desert-dwelling Fremen to avoid a swift death in the barren dunes, the ingenious (but totally gross) body suit allows the wearer to recycle, distil and drink their own fluids, with minimal waste.

"It had to look like it really did function," notes West, who collaborated on the film's sartorial centrepiece with Morgan and concept artist Keith Christensen. "We came up with pumps in the boots that, with your motion from walking and running, would circulate all excreted body fluids into a kind of holding area. And we had these pouches where it would turn to gas, and then there were actually tubes going through these different layers that you can see in the suit, and the different openings for ventilation. The first time I showed Denis the stillsuit I knew, somehow, we had hit it."

Designed to fit like a glove, the stillsuits had to be built bespoke for a wide range of body types, each costume personalised with "little charms and hidden talismans". To ensure the actors didn't overheat under the baking Abu Dhabi sun, where temperatures could reach 40°C, each stillsuit was fitted with a cooling micro-layer between the skin and the costume "almost like a reverse wetsuit," says Morgan. "That's how we kept them dry and cool – we used a base layer that basically wicks the moisture away from the body." It worked, as West points out: "The actors never complained about it in the desert. So, to an extent, they were functional!"

The term 'modieval' could also apply to the film's dynamic, but low tech action. In Dune, the existence of personal shields that can only be penetrated by a slow moving object, like a blade, means close quarters swordplay is the only viable form of combat. "The shields force you to find a new way to fight, because you cannot land a fast blow," Villeneuve explains. "In a way, it's a superfast chess game. You have to perform a lot of moves to distract your opponent in order to find a way to bring a blade close to him, and kill him. It was very exciting to design." So exciting, in fact, that Villeneuve and fight choreographer Roger Yuan developed a second style, exclusively for Momoa's Duncan Idaho. "That is more of a samurai approach, and inspired by Kurosawa, where you have stillness, and very few blows, but the blows are very, very precise. That's a more advanced technique for a fighter like Duncan Idaho."

Following the messy middle ages combat of The King, Chalamet threw himself into training for Dune, shooting an early sparring session with Gurney that soon turns serious over the course of three days. "I was proud to do all of that fight," Chalamet says. "What was used in the movie has my stunt double, Lorenz [Hideyoshi Ruwwe], in some parts. But I was proud to at least shoot all of it." Chalamet might not look like a typical action lead, a fact the film will have some fun with, but Paul's proficiency lies in speed and strategy, not strength. "One thing I will say about Timothée," Villeneuve offers. "He's not Jason Momoa – we were making jokes – but he is in a very great physical shape."

The first time I showed Denis the stillsuit I knew, somehow, we had hit it.

If Chalamet simply wanted to show off his fighting chops, there are half a dozen superhero films released every year he could have signed up for. What makes Dune different is that it’s wrestling with big themes that are just as relevant now as they were 56 years ago. "Dune is a love letter to ecology. And not in a tacky way," says Villeneuve, who hopes that the film will help young viewers discover Dune at a similarly formative time of their lives as he did. "[Herbert's] really someone who embraced ideas that are linked with ecosystems and evolution, and how to dramatise that in the most eloquent and poetic way."

As for Chalamet, the fact that a film of this scale was speaking to the world we live in made the project all the more irresistible. "With the year and a half that we've all had, there's going to be an appetite for projects that are truth-telling," he notes. "Dune is something that, although written in the '60s, recognised the ransacking of the Earth was not without physical consequence, a lot of which we're dealing with now. You see that with the way the Harkonnen treat Dune; the colonisation of the planet is relevant to a lot of the conversations we’re having today about the present consequences of the everlasting power structures of oppression. It speaks to the planet's plight at large."

Which brings us to the sandworm sized elephant in the room when it comes to Dune: the film everyone will see in October is only half the story. As Villeneuve puts plainly, "There's no such thing as Dune 1 and Dune 2. It's Dune: Part One and Dune: Part Two." But that hoped-for sequel isn't a sure thing. Villeneuve's films typically over perform commercially, but Blade Runner 2049 – a similarly cerebral, adult sci-fi – fell notably short at the box office. So what does Part One have to achieve for Part Two to become a reality?

"We have been hearing in the past few decades that it's not possible to adapt this book, and that it’s an impossible task. I think that in the back of the mind of the studio, it's still the same!" Villeneuve says with a hearty laugh. "So the first thing was to prove that there was a beautiful, popular movie that can exist, and I think that I proved that – everybody at Warner Bros and Legendary, they are 100 percent behind the project. They feel that it would need a really bad outcome at the box office to not have a Dune: Part Two, because they love the movie. They are proud of the movie, so they want the movie to move forward. And they still did half of it. So, you know, I’m very optimistic."

Dune's future prospects have been further complicated by the still-raging pandemic, and streaming service HBO Max, on which the film will debut on the same day it releases in cinemas in the US. Villeneuve was a vocal objector to the decision, penning a coruscating open letter shortly after the news broke. It's a move he's still not at peace with. "First of all, the enemy of cinema is the pandemic. That's the thing. We understand that the cinema industry is under tremendous pressure right now. That I get," Villeneuve concedes adding, however, "The way it happened, I'm still not happy. Frankly, to watch Dune on a television, the best way I can compare it is to drive a speedboat in your bathtub. For me, it's ridiculous. It's a movie that has been made as a tribute to the big-screen experience."

Despite the rocky road to screens so far, the fact that Dune will soon be opening the Venice Film Festival, nearly two months before it's released in cinemas, is a clear sign of confidence that positive word of mouth will follow. While the cast, all of whom have seen the film (some multiple times) can't help but offer rave reviews. "We're just extremely excited to get it out there, and are chomping at the bit, because of the delays," says Chalamet, who, much like Paul, already sees the future. "Talking with Denis and also Zendaya, we've really been excited about where these characters will go."

As for Villeneuve, he's currently hard at work on that return trip, praying to the makers that enough people share his dreams. "I'm writing [Part Two] now, and I feel like I'm eight years old again," he says, flashing a childlike grin. "That's very uncommon for me. It's the first time I've experienced it where I'm watching one of my movies, and I have a moment of deep gratitude, of deep joy, and I say, 'Thank you, life, for having allowed me to bring that to the screen.' [laughs] I don't know how other people will feel about it. But me? Denis Villeneuve when he was 14 years old? Thank you."

Dune 3 arrives in theaters on December 18. For more, check out our beginner's guide to the Dune books.

#3605. GTA 6 reportedly sets massive livestreaming record, watched more in its first week than Elden Ring, Diablo 4, Valorant, and Lost Ark combined

Grand Theft Auto 6 has broken another livestreaming record. After attracting more viewers across livestreaming platforms than any game ever on its launch day, Rockstar's open-world crime sim has reportedly continued to dominate on platforms like Twitch, YouTube, and Kick.

Over its first seven days on sale, GTA 6 has amassed over 420m hours watched, according to Streams Charts. That's nearly three times more than the previous record, held by Valorant's closed beta in April 2020. In fact, that 420m hours tally is more than the first-week watch time achieved by Valorant, Elden Ring, Diablo 4, and Lost Ark combined.

As for the livestreaming platforms that saw the largest audiences for GTA 6, YouTube reportedly had the lead in average audience numbers during the first six hours of launch, but Twitch took over in content volume in the days that followed. In fact, Twitch's GTA 6 watch time was higher at launch than any other game in its history.

Streams Charts also noted 1,056 channels reached new all-time peak viewership numbers while streaming GTA 6, in some cases multiplying their previous record tenfold. Major content creators like IShowSpeed, IlloJuan, and TheBurntPeanut stole the spotlight, but GTA 6 also helped many other channels set new viewership records.

Livestreaming, of course, isn't the only area where GTA 6 has set new records. Publisher Take-Two called it the biggest entertainment launch in history, generating $3.79bn (£2.89bn) in revenue from 32.5m copies sold on day one. Other parts of the industry have benefited, too. Anticipation for GTA 6 boosted US hardware sales for both PlayStation and Xbox, just as GTA 6 became each console brand's most pre-ordered title ever. At launch, more than 39 million people played GTA 6 on PS5, according to Sony. The game also had the highest number of concurrent players ever on any PlayStation console, beating even the most popular free-to-play titles.

You can check out Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough if you're in need of assistance, which we just updated today with a guide on how to whistle in GTA 6 - something I didn't know you could do. The walkthrough also covers other lesser-known mechanics such as how to steal ATMs in GTA 6, and much more besides.

#3602. "Where's the ding?!!" - I asked the PowerWash Simulator 2 team what they thought of Jason's nozzle work in GTA 6

Among the many, many side activities you can do in GTA 6, there's powerwashing. Relatively early on, as part of Chapter 1's Down to Earth mission, Jason whips out his nozzle and blasts Brian's boat to a gleaming sheen. Disappointingly for powerwashing fans, though, it's a bit of a one-and-done gag, never to return. But powerwashing is powerwashing, and we immediately wondered what the experts made of it all. Had Rockstar, with its legendary attention to detail, accurately captured the intricacies of powerwashing in those leisurely moments of carefree squirting?

A question had been asked and an answer was required. So who better to cast judgement on the authenticity of Jason's sway-and-spraying than FuturLab, the studio behind the delightfully zen PowerWash Simulator series? Thus, in a moment of whimsy, I asked if it might like to 'review' GTA 6's hosiest activity. At best, I was hoping for a cheeky little statement; I certainly wasn't expecting a big chunk of the PowerWash Simulator 2 team to join in the fun. "Fair to say," the intermediary PR noted, "the Futurlab team was excited about this one!"

So what's the verdict? Let us turn to the pros. "They've got the sounds and satisfaction of clearly a nice shiny flat surface just right," PowerWash Simulator 2 lead game designer Nick McCarthy opined, "but where's the ding!? 0/10, needs 200 percent more layers of muck and 20 percent more parkour." And quickly a trend emerged. "Great visuals, satisfying feel, but lacks the crucial ding and went by too quickly to listen to a podcast," senior programmer Will Dyball wrote. Then still more sadness for the lack of PowerWash Simulator's most motivating sound: "Didn't hear a ding," associate publishing producer Jess Crosby wrote. "Must have missed a bit."

A few team members also spotted some powerwashing faux pas. "No soap?" wrote 3D artist Eilidh Norris. "Rookie mistake, Jason." Programmer Jordan Lewis also reckoned Jason was making things unnecessarily hard for himself: "[He'd] have had an easier time had he taken the time to upgrade his washer and purchased some more nozzles," they wrote. "PS. Soap would have gotten that off in a flash." Others had safety concerns: "I find Jason's lack of protective overalls disturbing," said 3D artist Rory Peace, and data principal Russell Young agreed. "Clean speedboat, ruined clothes. Don't want to bring them 'Down to Earth', but we need to talk about PPE." People advisor Sarah Robshaw, meanwhile, spotted a more heinous omission: "Where's the cats????"

Elsewhere, game designer Sam Jenkins was delighted by the powerwashing representation. "I'm so glad that the Art of Powerwashing is being taken more seriously in mainstream games!" they wrote. "However, I think the dirt on the boat is too scarce for that satisfying cleaning contrast to come through."

Jenkins even had some expert suggestions to make Jason's little squirt-out more rewarding: "Maybe the boat should have been left in a flooded warehouse for 30 years to coat it in grime?" they continued. "Or even have a crushed fruit festival come through town to get some nice big colourful blobs all over the boat. Ooh! And we could even have the boat be the home of various squids to get some difficult-to-clean Ink streaked down it too!" Truly the words of someone who takes their powerwashing seriously!

Junior build engineer Owen Layton, programmer Jordan Lewis, and lead designer Nick McCarthy also provided 'reviews' in pictoral form, but technical complications mean they'll just have to exist in your imagination. Senior narrative designer Mark Ginbey, though, expressed admiration for all the in-world encouragement players are given. "Some excellent motivational text updates from Cal, like 'Mmhmm, half way there...' to indicate 50 percent completion," they wrote. "But Jason needs to concentrate on the work in hand. A quality powerwasher never talks on the job."

Senior game designer António Salreta had praise for GTA 6, with one exception: "It's an amazing game with so many fun systems - but. Needs. More. Nozzles." And how's this for a ringing endorsement from senior QA tester Paul Comse? "I love coming home after a hard day of work powerwashing in PowerWash Sim and unwinding by powerwashing some more in GTA," they wrote. But if we're scoring Jason's efforts? "7.8/10, too much water."

So there you go! The experts have spoken, and I'd call it a success for Rockstar's inaugural attempt at powerwashing, despite a handful of 'must try harders'. An unexpectedly generous response indeed! And if you're curious how FuturLab does it, look no further than last year's PowerWash Simulator 2. And for help with powerwashing in GTA 6, we've got a guide.

Earlier this year, rumours began to circulate that a remake of The Simpsons: Hit & Run was in the works, rumours which were lent further credence after Simpsons creator Matt Groening implied that a return of the PS2-era GTA clone was on the cards. Now though, it appears that this ephemeral project may have been scrapped as part of a larger swath of cancellations.

On LinkedIn (via Eurogamer) game designer Darren Evenson announced that he had been let go from New Radical Games, a studio formed from the ashes of Radical Entertainment, which developed The Simpsons: Hit & Run as well as the open-world superhero game Prototype. New Radical was rumoured to be working on a redux of Hit & Run, but it seems that, if that was indeed the case, it no longer is.

"It seems that not even a fantastic project with an incredible team is immune from the current state of the industry right now, as what we were working on at New Radical Games (although mind blowingly awesome) was part of a whole gaggle of cancellations. A gaggle I say!" Evenson wrote. He then added: "Oh you silly suits with spreadsheets… will you EVER learn? If you don't make the game, you can't make the money…and if you don't make the money then you don't get the power…and… well, there's more to that quote, but I digress."

As for why this post may refer to The Simpsons: Hit & Run, alongside New Radical's historical connection to the tie-in, Evenson's post contains several phrases that echo lines spoken in the TV Show. For example, in the episode Marge be Not Proud Troy McClure says "Oh, Shakazaramesh, will you ever learn?", while in Lisa's Rival, Homer protects a pile of sugar, saying "In America, first you get the sugar, then you get the power, then you get the women." This latter line is itself a reference to the movie Scarface, however, and Radical Entertainment also worked on a Scarface game, so it still isn't wholly clear what project Radical was working on.

It also isn't clear why the project was cancelled, or which publisher cancelled it. But Evenson says that he's now looking for work as a result of the project's premature end. "Please reach out, shout out, or perform some interpretive dance if you know of an opportunity that a hip cat like me could groove to."

#3600. GTA 6 causes surge in UK physical game sales, despite there being no disc in the box

Grand Theft Auto 6 has had a huge effect on physical game sales in the UK, despite not actually containing a disc in the box.

NielsenIQ data shows that GTA 6 drove boxed software sales up an enormous 409 percent for the launch period ending 21st November, compared to the previous week, resulting in the biggest week for UK physical game sales since Christmas 2018.

GTA 6 alone accounted for £32m of the total £43m boxed software sales, apparently - around 74 percent, with 88 percent of its sales generated on day-one. But it's not a champion or record-breaker in this regard. In fact, GTA 6 places 17th in the all-time table of first-week boxed revenue, which is refreshingly humbling given the money-making records it's been breaking elsewhere. This is to do with the overwhelming shift towards buying games digitally, of course.

Nevertheless, Rockstar is well represented in the all-time list (which stretches back to 1995), because it's none other than GTA 5 that sits at the top, and GTA 4 at 11th.

But the GTA 6 effect is that of a rising tide, with console hardware sales rising 38 percent, to their highest level since 2025. Specifically, PS5 sales rose 46 percent and Xbox Series sales jumped a considerable 75 percent. And it's been a similar result in the US, where PS5 and Xbox Series sales have more than doubled.

Gaming accessory sales also got a boost, with PS5 controller sales up 355 percent, gaming headset sales up 94 percent, and - more nichely - gaming chair sales up 32 percent, which is apparently in line with the 40 percent increase they experienced around GTA 5.

"While the physical games market looks very different today compared with previous blockbuster launches, GTA 6 has still made a huge impact," said NielsenIQ's Dorian Bloch. "Back in 2008, boxed software accounted for half of all games retail revenue for the combined sectors of software, hardware, and gaming accessories, compared with 15 percent so far in 2026. This is a reflection of the market increasingly shifting towards digital downloads."

It's against this backdrop, of course, that Sony made its hugely controversial decision to wind down production of PlayStation game discs starting January 2028. This has led to boycotts and backlash and much angry sentiment towards the company, but Grand Theft Auto 6's enormous digital success is likely to be a hard example to ignore.
