One person who has been the talk of the town in the world of celebrity fashion is Julianne Hough. As Dancing with the Stars aired its 35th season on the 2026 TV schedule, she made some very bold outfit choices, and in response, fans did not hold back their opinions on them. Now, her stylist has spoken out about the critical discourse regarding the co-host’s DWTS ensembles.

I’ll be the first to admit that when Julianne Hough walked into the ballroom for a given episode of DWTS, I was often shocked by her outfits. They were bold, sometimes avant-garde and always fun to see. According to her stylist, Brad Goreski, they were trying going for fits that were “super elevated and strong” as well as “super extravagant and wild and playful and colorful and sparkly.” I think they achieved that goal, as you can see in the photos of Hough and her co-host Alfonso Ribeiro below:

The co-host’s fashion choices throughout the season (which you can see with a Disney+ subscription) led to quite a bit of criticism from fans. One person posted one of Hough’s sheer outfits on Instagram and wrote over it, “Respectfully, who is Julianne’s stylist and why do they need to be fired?” Meanwhile, someone on X said they thought the people dressing Hough were “playing a cruel joke” on her. These kinds of comments happened week after week.

When Goreski and Hough spoke to Glamour about her style this season, they addressed the backlash that came with it too. The dancer’s stylist said he has “an awareness” of it. He also explained:

And I love it. Any conversation, good or bad, around fashion is great. I think people weighing in—they like the hair but not the dress; they thought it was a bad outfit; they think she should fire me—is totally fine, because we’re really excited by what we’re doing, and we put a lot of thought and energy into it. I think Jules ultimately brings the looks to life, and I’m glad that there’s another part of the show that people talk about. Not every person’s going to love every look. I know that from being a stylist for 15 years. And that’s okay.

Well, that’s certainly a good mentality to have about all this. Along with that, Hough noted that evolving her style came with risk too. Millions of people watch DWTS, and as her stylist explained, not everyone will like her looks. So, with that being said, the co-host stated that her motto this season was “apathy is the enemy.” She also had this to say about how people react to her fashion choices:

The reason things exist and have charge and stay visible [is] people either love it or hate it. They still want to talk about it.

To that point, there were lots of moments on DWTS this year that got people on the internet talking, like liftgate, Jennifer Lawrence trolling Connor Wood, and Ezra Frech making it through his freestyle after his prosthetic fell off. Overall, Season 35 was met with a whole lot of love, but also quite a bit of intense discourse too. And yes, part of that had to do with Julianne Hough's fashion choices.

However, as both the co-host and her stylist said, part of the fun of fashion is getting people talking about it.

#3597. Nioh and Ninja Gaiden studio is using AI for QA, but argues "that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands"

Team Ninja (Nioh, Ninja Gaiden) is the latest game development studio to implement AI into some of its workflow, but producer Kohei Shibata still believes that fun games need to be "crafted by human hands."

The producer best known for the tough-as-nails Nioh trilogy and Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty spoke about the controversial tech during South Korea's GCON 2026, in an interview with INVEN Global. "Currently, we utilize AI in QA and various verification tasks to streamline certain workflows," Shibata explained.

He went on to argue that if AI can "shorten task times," then developers can spend more hours "elevating the game's overall quality" in other ways. "In that sense, using AI is beneficial." Team Ninja isn't fully on board with enforcing the tech elsewhere, though: "Since it's still a new technology, we are continuously evaluating the most appropriate ways to implement it. I imagine other game companies are facing similar questions." (Good spot, Kotaku.)

"What matters fundamentally is that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands. Repetitive, simple tasks that anyone must perform can be streamlined using technology. But ultimately, deciding how to craft the game and what makes it enjoyable must be done by humans. Using AI itself should never become the goal. I believe the principle that humans must think for themselves and finish the game will remain unchanged in the future," Shibata continued.

Generative AI's use in game development is still a hotly debated topic among both players and the people making games, but it's been prevalent nonetheless. A recent report estimated that around 40 percent of game developers were using AI in some fashion, even if lots of them also agreed the tech was harmful. Bigger publishers like Ubisoft and Epic Games are more aggressively pursuing an AI-first future, too.

Team Ninja seems to be settling into a middle ground, at least, according to Shibata's statement. Speaking on the studio's approach to difficult games, he said that a player's failure should never be the game's fault. Dying in a game like Ninja Gaiden or Nioh should always be the result of human error, otherwise death "causes frustration." Finding that perfect, often bloody sweet spot is something only humans can do.

Even a fair few Rockstar Games workers felt like GTA 6's launch day "would never come," according to co-studio head and lead developer Rob Nelson.

The wait for GTA 6 was agonizingly long for some corners of the video game world - it's been 13 years since GTA 5, eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, and four years since we glimpsed the first set of leaks. The protracted development even led to at least one incredibly popular meme: 'We got X before GTA 6.'

But GTA 6 hopefuls weren't alone in the feeling - many employees at Rockstar Games felt the same way, apparently.

In an interview with GamesRadar+ ahead of launch, Nelson said "it feels surreal" to see the game finally rolling out across the world. "I think a lot of us felt like the day would never come. A lot of us, certainly on the senior team, have shipped a fair few games. But it's been a while since we've done one of these and this one took a good chunk of time to sort of figure it out.

"I think it's surreal, it's a relief – we're very nervous, when you get really close to something maybe your perspective is a little bit compromised [laughter]. But yeah, we're in a little bit of disbelief and we probably will be until release, and then hopefully it'll become real once people are talking about it and playing it," he continued.

And, boy, are there a lot of people playing this thing. Parent company Take-Two announced that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies before it even launched and made almost $4 billion by the end of its first day of release. The publisher has yet to reveal updated figures, but this is easily the biggest entertainment launch in history.

If you're playing now, be sure to check out our GTA 6 guide to learn everything there is to know about the fastest cars and how to get a rhino tank.

#3595. Team Ninja Is Using AI For Quality Assurance, But Insists Creative Choices ‘Must Be Done By Humans’

Team Ninja is known, in part, for developing difficult games, but producers Kohei Shibata and Masakazu Hirayama emphasized during an interview with INVEN Global at GCON 2026 in South Korea that thereâs a key difference between difficult and unfair. The pair also spoke about how the Koei Tecmo subsidiary approaches the use of AI in games development, and an awkward compromise between implementing the technology for repetitive QA tasks, while arguing that “what matters fundamentally is that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands.”

Shibata and Hirayama are best known for their work as producers on the Nioh and Wo Long series respectively, two games that take the combat-driven difficulty of the iconic Ninja Gaiden franchise and transpose it onto the world of samurai and Chinese mythology. Before the topic of AI arose, the two discussed the crucial role of player interaction and movement in their games, beginning with the similarities between all three franchises and most notably their swordplay and the focus on timing your attacks and reading an opponentâs next move. According to both, this process of requiring a player to learn an enemyâs next move and counter is key to straddling the line between challenging and frustrating play.

âI consider Nioh to be samurai action,â explained Shibata. âSamurai combat involves stillness and movement. You stand firmly grounded, observing the opponent’s moves, and deliver a sharp strike the instant an opening appears.â Meanwhile, for Hirayama on Wo Long, that game was defined by âaggressive Chinese martial arts action,â where âattack and defense flow together seamlesslyâ and where âaggressively attacking is important, but defense must also lead directly into the next attack.â

The two go on to argue that it’s important to make a game that is polished in a way that reduces friction between a player’s action and consequence. If a person fails, it must be their fault, not the game’s. âI believe [the core essence of action games is] control responsiveness,â Shibata explained. âWhen a player presses a button, the character must move exactly as they intended. If you press a button and the character doesn’t react properly, it causes frustration. Conversely, if a slight input causes an exaggerated movement, it feels awkward. Therefore, responsiveness to input must be simple and intuitive, and the movement must be communicated rapidly.â

We have seen numerous studios speak out in recent times about where they will and wonât use AI. While some Japanese developers are embracing the technology, others are more cautious, either avoiding it entirely or insisting they only use the technology for optimizing their development framework while leaving creative choices to humans. The latter is the direction being taken by Capcom with its next generation of RE Engine, and appears to also be the choice being made by Team Ninja, who are already using AI for QA purposes.

As Shibata explained, âCurrently, we utilize AI in QA and various verification tasks to streamline certain workflows. If we can use AI to shorten task times, we can dedicate that saved time toward elevating the game’s overall quality. In that sense, using AI is beneficial. However, since it is still a new technology, we are continuously evaluating the most appropriate ways to implement it. I imagine other game companies are facing similar questions.” He continued,

What matters fundamentally is that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands. Repetitive, simple tasks that anyone must perform can be streamlined using technology. But ultimately, deciding how to craft the game and what makes it enjoyable must be done by humans. Using AI itself should never become the goal. I believe the principle that humans must think for themselves and finish the game will remain unchanged in the future.

Where, if anywhere, is an acceptable use of AI is a topic that remains up for debate, but it appears many developers are settling into a space where it is used to handle repetitive tasks. The use of AI in QA actually predates the modern conversations of generative AI, and doesnât necessarily rely on the tech: Sony, for instance, has been experimenting with AI for many years to test games. Whether this is something audiences are willing to tolerate, or indeed is something that will further threaten jobs in the games industry, remains to be seen.

#3594. The Witcher 3's new patch adds 40 cross-platform mods, fixes plenty of game-breaking bugs and "various lighting issues"

"The Path never sleeps, and the work is never done."

Developer CD Projekt Red has rolled out a new patch for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered on all platforms, which squashes dozens of bugs and adds 40 cross-platform mods with "more on the way."

"Two things are certain in a witcher's life: the Path never sleeps, and the work is never done," the studio wrote in its latest exhaustive list of patch notes for the decade-old game.

Patch 5.02's handiest changes come from those aforementioned bug fixes, many of which once caused the game to crash entirely or simply not work as intended. One such bug caused "time to go backwards indefinitely." Another turned Geralt bald. Opening the game with outdated mods could also result in a crash on PC. All of those, plus plenty more, have been fixed.

When The Witcher 3 Remastered first dropped, many players also took issue with the game's updated and sometimes "lifeless" lighting. Previous CDPR patches already targeted the lighting changes in question, but this newest patch continues to fix "various lighting issues across multiple locations and cutscenes."

The studio specifically names "overly bright or dark areas" and "inconsistent lighting transitions and flickering."

The Witcher 3's free remastered upgrade also gave all console owners access to mod support, though not all pre-existing PC mods were available to download for console folks. This patch is expanding the selection somewhat with 40 new cross-platform mods, including glowy eyes for Geralt and a new monster hunt - and on social media, the studio promised "more on the way."

CD Projekt Red is still hard at work on two big upcoming sequels, The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2. Speaking on the former in a recent earnings call, joint-CEO Michal Nowakowski said we can expect a similar leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4 as we've just seen from GTA 5 to GTA 6.

Team Ninja producer Kohei Shibata has revealed that the studio behind Nioh and Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty uses AI in its development processes. But he stressed that games should still ultimately be crafted by humans.

Speaking to INVEN Global at South Korea's CGON 2026 (via Eurogamer), Shibata said that the studio uses "AI in QA and various verification tasks to streamline certain workflows."

Shibata argued that if AI can "shorten task times" then developers can focus their efforts on "elevating the game's overall quality," although he caveated that "since it's still a new technology, we are continuously evaluating the most appropriate ways to implement it."

One thing Shibata emphasises, however, is that the quality of a game still rests upon human-centred design. "What matters fundamentally is that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands. Repetitive, simple tasks that anyone must perform can be streamlined by technology. But ultimately, deciding how to craft the game and what makes it enjoyable must be done by humans."

He also pointed out that "using AI itself should never become the goal. I believe the principle that humans must think for themselves and finish the game will remain unchanged in the future."

It's frustrating that Shibata doesn't go into detail about what he means by "AI" here. The term is now applied to an extremely broad range of technologies alongside large-scale LLMs, and this reveal doesn't necessarily mean Team Ninja is getting ChatGPT to do its QA for it. Back in October, Capcom announced that it planned to turn the RE Engine into an "AI generation game engine" but what it meant was it was implementing machine-learning tech into its engine to improve its performance and data handling, and not that it was pivoting to AI-generating Leon Kennedy or whatever.

Presumably, Team Ninja's application of AI runs along similar lines, but it's hard to say without knowing specifics. Either way, this is not to dismiss people's concerns about AI's growing presence in game development. A recent survey of game developers reported that, while 40% of developers have now used AI at some point, more than half believe the tech is having a negative impact on the games industry. Many of these negative impacts are easy to spot, too, from Steam being inundated with AI slop, to PC hardware becoming increasingly unaffordable.

Well-deserved praise hit the internet, and people on X are already ready to see them perform in February:

I'll admit I said the same thing after watching, especially after seeing how it was executed. There were no fancy set pieces as we've seen at past Super Bowl shows, or big cameos lined up. It was just the rap group plus the late Ol' Dirty Bastard's son (Young Dirty Bastard) performing some of their most beloved hits, with a crowd on the field hyping them up.

Wu-Tang Clan's Method Man: His Best Contributions To Movies, TV And Hip-Hop

I was already hyped about the performance going into things, but it exceeded my expectations by a lot. I have to give some props to former Super Bowl performer Eminem, who produced the show and could've easily inserted himself into it as a fellow hip-hop icon and well-known celebrity from Detroit. Fortunately, he showed some restraint and allowed the veteran New York rappers to have the spotlight in what will go down as a memorable performance.

It has me thinking about Jay-Z's upcoming performance, and how people could inevitably compare what he does to this. Hov has claimed he's largely disconnected from social media, though I'm curious if his team is aware of how the show was received and if they're thinking about how they can attempt to replicate it or ensure he has just as much success.

Super Bowl halftime shows are always under scrutiny regardless of who's performing, but it feels like the bar has been raised. An acclaimed halftime rap performance just months away from his own is going to have people wondering if he can rise to the occasion, including me. I hate to say I'm skeptical the rap legend can deliver, but I feel like nostalgia for his music has not aged nearly as well as the Wu-Tang Clan's.

We shall see if that's the case when Jay-Z takes the stage during the Super Bowl on February 14th. Yes, that is Valentine's Day, and yes, I'm already waiting for the stories of couples who don't realize that until it's too late.

Star Trek is his main jam, but he also regularly reports on happenings in the world of Star Trek, WWE, Doctor Who, 90 Day Fiancé, Quantum Leap, and Big Brother. He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

The Saudi Arabian investment group is struggling to turn a profit from its investment in renowned Japanese developer SNK, as the 48-year-old company faces heavy losses following lower than expected sales. However, it might have have found a new medium through which to claw back its cash: the movies. After all, SNK’s series likeÂ Fatal Fury, The King of Fighters and Metal Slug still hold cultural capital. Amidst Saudi Arabiaâs many other investments is new film studio The Arena, which has just announced Metal Slug as the latest property from the game studio to be in the works for a movie adaptation.

First reported by Variety, the studio announced that the adaptation of the side-scrolling military action platformer is going ahead, withÂ I Love My Dad director James Morosini attached to the project. An initial plot loosely based on the already thin narrative of theÂ Metal Slug series has also been revealed, centered on a misfit quartet of army recruits known as Marco Rossi, Tarma Roving, Eri Kasamoto and Fio Germi, as they stand up to General Morden to save the world from evil. #3590. EA removes some live service fluff from Skate and ends seasonal structure "in favour of regular, agile content updates"

EA is ditching seasonal updates and shaving some of the live service fluff off Skate (for some reason stylised as skate.) going forward. Normally, such news would be cause for concern. Here, the publisher assured players the transition will lead to more regular updates since devs can now push out new features without waiting for the next season to roll around.

"EA and Full Circle are committed to keep driving skate. forward. Just as a reminder, we're still very much in Early Access," the studio wrote in a new blog post. "The game is still a work in progress, and we're using this valuable time to experiment, iterate, and figure out what works best for the long-term health of the game - especially when it comes to social features and progression. Ultimately, we want to build skate. in a way that lets us roll out fresh content much faster, even if it's not totally finished yet."

Skate's fifth and final season is coming to an end on 1st December, with Full Circle embracing a different model from there on out. "We are transitioning away from the traditional seasonal cadence in favor of regular, agile content updates," it explained.

Full Circle is also throwing out the skating sim's version of a seasonal battle pass (horribly named skate.Pass) by the end of the year, and will rethink how the game's progression system works: "We've said it many times: we have a long-term future vision for skate, and this is a key part of it. Update 0.33.1 will be our very first update in this post-season era."

The move away from rigid seasonal updates "gives the development team the freedom to launch features earlier in their lifecycle," the blog post continued. "This means we can deploy work-in-progress mechanics and gather your direct feedback to continuously shape and build upon San Vansterdam. We've started this with in-game testing of features such as Spot Battles, Block Parties, and Prox Chat before rolling it out officially, and we’re going to continue with this process."

Full Circle's live service rejig also means the in-game currency Tix is being retired, and some maps will no longer be locked behind paywalls. Skate still has real-money microtransactions and a cosmetics store, though it's nice to see some of the more aggressive live service bits being plucked out.

The holidays are in full swing, and for Meghan Markle, that means starting some new traditions across the pond. Considering the Duke and Duchess of Sussex relocated to the UK earlier this year, their holidays have been looking just a tad different. However, despite no longer living in the U.S., Markle still made sure to celebrate Thanksgiving, and I just learned about some of the tips and tricks she has for hosting.

When it comes to Thanksgiving and Christmas, hosting people can be overwhelming. And while Markle and Prince Harry are still trying to find their forever home, that is not stopping them from being good hosts. The Suits alum told People that she picked up a thing or two while working in the restaurant business before hitting it big that she applies to her holiday hosting, and this piece of advice might just be the most important one:

Being a great host is all about anticipating your guests’ needs — something I learned working in restaurants and now love bringing into my own home. With a little thoughtful planning, you can make everyone feel comfortable and cared for.

Markle is no stranger to making sure her guests feel comfortable, as fans have seen on her lifestyle series, With Love, Meghan (which you can stream with a Netflix subscription). Additionally, she worked at the coat check of a Chicago bar while attending Northwestern University, so she knows what it takes to make a good environment. Speaking of environment, setting the mood is a very important part of creating a good one, and according to Markle, candles are a key part of that:

Light a few candles — choose scented ones to set the mood in the living areas and unscented for the kitchen (in those spaces, let the fragrance of the food shine).

Meanwhile, hosting does not mean doing things alone, especially for a holiday like Thanksgiving when so much prep has to be done. On that note, Markle stressed the importance of doing a bit of extra work ahead of time. Even with kids, they’re never too young to assist, no matter how big or small the work is:

Chop your veggies and herbs in advance to save time on the day, and also for those finishing touches, whether you’re serving homemade or store-bought dishes. Your kids can join in too! They can proudly say they helped.

Markle and Prince Harry are parents to Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, and I can’t imagine how chaotic the holidays are with two young children running around the house. Not to mention that things are a bit different now that they’ve moved. I do, however, love that Markle includes her kids in the Thanksgiving prep. Plus, it keeps the children busy and makes them feel included, so I definitely will keep that tip in mind.

Including the kids and working on the veggies early is not the only advice Markle had when it came to food prep. The former actress had plenty to share about the most important Thanksgiving tradition, the food, and even confessed to one aspect that her own husband is a fan of, so much so that he would not let her live it down if she hadn’t brought it up:

Top tip on the carrots — keep the tops and blend them with parmesan, olive oil and pine nuts for a refreshing take on pesto to elevate your holiday spread. Served with creamy mashed potatoes, a green salad speckled with flower sprinkles and rich gravy (my husband would never forgive me if I didn’t add that to the table), this is sure to please your entire gathering.

Of course, everyone does prep in their own way, but I do love hearing these great tips from Markle. Plus, these tricks give us a peek into how the Duke and Duchess take on the holidays.

The couple plans to spend Christmas in the UK, just like Thanksgiving, and I wouldn’t be surprised if the prep was already beginning. However, clearly Meghan Markle knows how to take it all in stride.

#3587. Marvelous, developer of the Story of Seasons series, opens up voluntary redundancy scheme as it seeks to reduce headcount by 65 employees

The offer is described as an "early retirement" program.

Marvelous, the studio known for its work on the Story of Seasons series as well as the upcoming Eternal Anima, has announced the introduction of a voluntary redundancy scheme. Through this program, it's aiming to lower its headcount by 65 employees.

Per Automaton, this "early retirement" program is part of an effort to restructure its console business, which refers to non-mobile, non-live-service games under its umbrella.

The reason for this change is the shifting environment in game development, namely the growing scope of development and elongated development cycles. The company cites a need to optimise its workforce and shift towards flexibility, per the introduction of the early retirement program.

Marvelous will begin gathering applications, with those choosing to take the company up on the offer set to leave at the end of the financial year in March 2027. These employees will receive a bonus as part of their redundancy package, as well as assistance finding new employment elsewhere if they desire it.

Marvelous emphasised that despite this program, it still sees console game development as one of its core businesses. This comes in the same financial year Marvelous reported a 1,105 percent increase in profit between April 2026 - September 2026, credited to overseas sales of both new indie releases and older console games.

Night Street Games' team-based shooter may not be perfect, but it is pretty clever.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Rick and Ted have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager.

It's been a tough old year for competitive multiplayer shooters. We've seen Highguard fail, Marathon struggle, 1047 Games flail futilely around with Splitgate: Arena Reloaded and Empulse. Even Arc Raiders has bitten the bullet and admitted that its players simply do not want to shoot one another. In fact, were it not for Wardogs bucking this grim trend, you could build a strong case to say that 2026 is the year competitive multiplayer shooting died.

Among the pile of casualties awaiting revival from a medic is Last Flag, the competitive, capture-the-flag shooter developed by Night Street Games, a studio founded by Imagine Dragons' lead singer Dan Reynolds, and his brother and band manager Mac Reynolds. Released back in April, Last Flag ran into the cold shoulder of the market almost immediately, and within two months of launch, Night Street ceased development and laid off half its staff.

Rather than pull Last Flag offline, however, Night Street decided to put the game's future in the hands of players by adding the ability to host custom lobbies alongside the already-existing bot support, and slashing the price. I decided to take this life-support version of Last Flag for a spin, and it's a damn shame this game didn't grab an audience, because it's a ton of fun.

Now, I won't pretend to be baffled as to why Last Flag didn't grab people's attention. At a glance it resembles that infamous Randy Pitchford tweet about Battleborn. It mixes capture-the-flag with hide-and-seek, hero shooters, control-point domination, all with character art direction that screams: "My voice lines are going to annoy the shit out of you!"

But just as a list of ingredients does not make a meal, a list of features does not make a game. The way Last Flag puts these elements together is fairly ingenious—producing a style of multiplayer that doesn't really feel like any other game.

A round of Last Flag starts with a minute-long hide phase, where one player from each team is selected to hide their team's flag somewhere in their half of the map. Last Flag's maps are holier than a Swiss cheese blessed by the Pope, their undulating landscapes riddled with apertures, cutouts and tunnels perfectly suited for squirrelling away a flag in.

Once both flags are hidden, the match begins in earnest, and both teams set out to capture the other team's flag. But of course, unlike traditional CTF, neither team knows where their opponents' flag is.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

There are a couple of ways to track down the flag. But if you want, you can just roam around enemy territory looking for it. This is not ideal. Apart from the fact that you're likely to get gunned down by the opposing team, maps are pretty roomy, so you're unlikely to stumble upon the flag by chance.

This is where the control points come in. There are three control points that each team can conquer, and holding a control point does three things. It lets you respawn there, which is handy for getting back into the fight. It can help heal players, as each control point generates a healing radius. But most importantly, it will narrow down the search area for the flag.

See, Last Flag features a grid-based minimap showing both team's territory. If you hold a control point, some of those squares will be coloured red or blue to show where the Flag isn't. The more control points you hold, the faster the squares get eliminated, and the quicker you can track down the flag.

This mechanic is Last Flag's main spark of inspiration, as it transforms each round from a relatively aimless game of hide-and-seek into a much more structured affair where the tension escalates constantly. Each minute that ticks by, the chance that your flag gets discovered increases. The combination of CTF and domination also introduces an element of tactics. Do you prioritise the control points to narrow down the flag's location as quickly as possible? Or do you scour enemy territory and try to get ahead of those invisible timers?

Even once the flags are found, you still essentially have the actual capture-the-flag part to play. Your team must capture and hold the enemy flag for a set amount of time before you'll be declared victorious, so each round ends in an exciting base defence as you protect your stolen goods from a desperate enemy assault.

It's a really well thought-out ruleset, and much like Wardogs, takes a basic, familiar multiplayer shooter concept and reworks it into something that feels fresh and new. There are other fun touches too. Alongside the fact that each character has their own abilities, they can also upgrade those abilities during a match by shooting cashbots to earn some moola. As well as giving players something to do while searching for the flag, players can also hunt these unfortunate automatons during the hide phase, keeping them occupied while the flag is concealed.

I do have one gripe with Last Flag though: as a shooter, it's a bit unsatisfying. Bullet impacts sometimes feel vague and hard to read, and I do wonder whether the cartoonish art-style robs the game of some of its lethality.

Night Street Games may have been better off drawing more inspiration from Last Flag's arena-shooter roots, building a game that looked and felt a bit less Overwatch and a bit more Unreal Tournament. Or to split the difference and shoot for Team Fortress 2. Then again, many multiplayer shooters which have appealed to an older crew have also fallen flat on their flak-cannons, so you can understand why Night Street Games made the creative decisions it did.

Yet while Last Flag is flawed, it is most certainly not a cynical celebrity cash grab like, say, the Mr Beast x James Patterson novel that nobody apparently read. It's a game made by people with a clear understanding of and appreciation for the genre, looking to take it somewhere a little bit different. Night Street's experiment may not have been as successful as Wardogs, but that doesn't invalidate the attempt. Even without a community to support it, I would still say Last Flag is worth investigating for shooter aficionados.

#3584. Rockstar boss "so grateful" to have kept GTA 6's big prologue twist a secret - and reveals Tomás' story could have been very different

"Multiple times throughout development, people were like, 'Can it not be...'"

If you've played the first 20 minutes or so of Grand Theft Auto 6, you'll know there's a hugely significant plot revelation there - one Rockstar somehow managed to keep entirely secret until the game's launch.

It's somewhat miraculous they did, given the many leaks the studio has suffered until now. And while, frankly, the embargo restrictions around discussing it in our GTA 6 review made a deeper analysis of Jason and Lucia's story more than a little awkward, I'm also mostly glad it remained a surprise. It's one of the great twists delivered in a game of this kind.

Speaking to Eurogamer in an interview shortly before GTA 6 was released, Rockstar Games' head of development Rob Nelson discussed the secret and, notably, the fact the team also discussed going another way entirely.

Spoilers for GTA 6's opening half hour - and further backstory around that moment from later in the game - below.

The big twist of course is that Jason and Lucia have a young child, Tomás, who we see Lucia abandoning in order to rob a store at gunpoint during the game's prologue.

It's an astonishing moment, both in the complexity it immediately lends Lucia, who is at once painted in a more negative light as a result, and in the stakes it affords her and Jason. This is the first time GTA's protagonists have genuine, human stakes that underpin their actions during the game's story, and at the same time Rockstar, in doing so, opens a route for itself to offering a far more nuanced take on modern crime.

But it was also something of a risk – and a hotly debated one, as Nelson told me during our conversation – as giving the game's protagonists that kind of narrative weight ran somewhat counter to the crime movie, straight-to-the-action thrills of previous GTAs.

"I'm so grateful that we managed to keep that under wraps," Nelson said. The subversion of expectations was intentional. "You feel like you maybe know these characters, or what the game or the story is going to be about, and then in the first 10, 15 minutes, it takes on a completely different context."It was an idea that came about organically. "But the idea of the character wanting something that maybe is at odds with what you thought you wanted as a player coming in, which is amassing as much material wealth as possible, and as many cars, and as many things," he said, was something Rockstar found particularly compelling.

The next point of the studio's focus then became the justification for Lucia's decision, Nelson explained. "The story was always, broadly, going to go through some of the major beats that it did," once Rockstar decided on the key points of the protagonists being a couple and them having a child. "But the details of the relationship, the narrative details of it, we dialled in a lot - because we're doing a lot there. She's leaving a kid early on – that's not a very sympathetic move to make."

That led to the decision to show, later in the story, more about why Lucia opted to leave Tomás in that moment. "Many chapters later, where [Jason] is like: 'What? Why did you do that?' And she has a flashback to sort of being at her wit's end," Nelson said, which then flows into the question of why she left Jason in the first place. "Cal asks Jason, 'Why did she leave?' And so, well, she didn't know she was pregnant at the time. 'Okay, but why didn't she call you?' 'Well, because I might've told her I didn't want [to be a father].' So you have to just make sure that you can understand both of their perspectives."

The tension from the fact they had a child, and that the two of them were away from their son as you play the game, was significant enough to become a point of discussion within the studio.

"Multiple times throughout development, we had this child, and people are like, 'Can it not be, like, theirs?'" Nelson said. "'Could it be like her little sister? Could it be– because I really feel bad having a good time in Vice City…' and the questions are valid," he continued. "But it wouldn't be powerful if not. So it was up to us to figure out how [you resolve that tension]."

Like with Lucia's justification for leaving Tomás - revealed in a striking dream-slash-flashback later in the game, that mixes typically exaggerated Rockstar satire with genuine social commentary - this then led to a cascade of other character moments. "How about he's in a better position than he would ever be with them, and so he's with her aunt, who's way more stable, and has a loving husband and other little kids, and he's always having a good time?" Nelson said.

He points to a conversation between Jason and Lucia in the game's first chapter as another example. "Very early on, in chapter one, they have this chat where he's like, 'Let's FaceTime - FruitFace is the thing we use - and she's like, 'No, I don't want to confuse him. He's better off until we get our shit together.' And he's like 'Okay' and she's like, 'It's not a cop-out', and he's like, 'No, no, I met my father on the other side of a glass divider, so I'm kind of trying to break that cycle.' And that's right in chapter one, and so it's a thread all the way through."

The result, then, is that the decision to add Tomás ultimately shaped many of the key parts of Jason and Lucia's characters, from their relationships with their own parents – Jason's being in jail, and Lucia's mother too narcissistic to help – to what is, really, the entire narrative arc of the story. And rightly so; a child is a big deal, and one of many reasons why GTA 6 is able to tap into something deeper than any of the previous games in the series before.

We've much more from our interview with Rob Nelson to come over the following days. In the meantime, he discussed why Rockstar made a form of honour system a core part of GTA 6's design (spoiler: because thinking more deeply about your in-game choices is fun). And in other Rockstar news, the studio has surprised those keeping up with its ongoing unionisation efforts by voting against formal recognition of the Rockstar Game Workers' Union.

Mass Effect Andromeda suffered hugely because the studio chased procedural planet generation (think Starfield or No Man's Sky) for far too long, according to former Bioware producer Mark Darrah.

The Bioware veteran who had a hand in everything from Dragon Age to Anthem recently spoke to YouTuber Pembridge about the studio's historic run of games - including some of its best RPGs and the missteps that eventually paved the way for Bioware's closure and Mass Effect 5's cancellation.

Asked about what went wrong with Mass Effect Andromeda, Darrah points the finger at the game's scrapped procedural planet system. "Casey [Hudson], he loves Star Control," Darrah explains. "In the deep DNA of Mass Effect has always been this exploration, random planet thing. It's just that the franchise has never really done it."

"So I think before Casey left, he planted the seed of them doing this and they [the developers] chased that feature. They were still working on that feature into [...] late 2016, I guess, even though it was way too late for that," Darrah continues. Mass Effect Andromeda eventually launched in March 2017.

"That feature should have been cut completely and cut a year or two earlier - and it was eventually cut completely," he adds. "But the problem is when you chase a feature like that - and it essentially happened on Dragon Age 4 as well - is that a similar kind of feature gets chased way too long, and it and it prevents actual content."

Darrah explains that the studio believed the procedural planet generation would have made up a significant portion of Mass Effect Andromeda, so scrapping the feature late into development meant there wasn't enough time to create content that would have filled the void.

"If you believe that there is a procedural system coming online that's going to provide 40% of your content, 80% of your content, whatever the number is, you don't build the content that would go in the hole that's going to be left by the eventual cutting of that feature," Darrah says.

The holidays are a great time to be around family and celebrate their company, but they are always more difficult when you’ve just lost a loved one. Breaking Bad cast member RJ Mitte died on October 12, 2026, at the age of 34 by suicide. The loss is still fresh for his mother and sister, and they took some time to publicly pay tribute to him on Thanksgiving.

Mitte famously played the son of Walter White, Walter Jr., on the hit AMC show for five seasons along with a host of other roles. He was also a disability rights activist who spoke out about living with cerebral palsy since he was a toddler. Check out how his mother, Dyna Mitte, paid homage to her late son on Thursday:

A post shared by Dyna Mitte (@dyna_banana)

Mitte’s mom shared a photo of herself with RJ Mitte and his sister Lacianne Carriere. She wrote that she’s “missing” him on Thanksgiving, but she “made all [his] favorites”. RJ’s sister also took to her Instagram account to share a throwback photo with the late actor. Here it is:

RJ’s younger sister expressed that she’s “thankful for the time” she had with her brother, and is really feeling his absence on the first holiday she and her family are spending without him. About a month ago, Carriere took to the platform to share a long tribute to RJ, calling him her “everything” and “other half”. It’s a particularly huge loss for his closest relatives.

Mitte’s body was found by his mother on the morning of October 12 in his home in Brownville, Texas. His official cause of death was ruled a suicide the same day. His mother said she had offered and suggested her son go to therapy in the three months before his passing, but he said he was “OK” and “handling it” (via Today).

RJ’s mother said she would have dragged him “screaming and yelling” to seek professional help if she knew what would happen. His mom also said she thinks the suicide might have been a “spur of the moment” decision because he didn’t leave a note behind.

RJ Mitte had spent time with Breaking Bad co-star Luis Moncada shortly before his passing, and she expressed that the actor had been “struggling”. His mother said RJ had “already signed deals on several new movies”, was working on a book and was starting a food truck before his death. Mitte had also popped the question to his longtime girlfriend Kennedy Suarez a year ago.

The actor started on Breaking Bad at the age of 14 and continued to have a main role on the beloved series throughout its mind-blowing run. Through the role, he brought his experiences with cerebral palsy to television without it ever being central to his character.

Bryan Cranston spoke to the actor’s death by saying he was in “deep despair” at the news and recalled RJ Mitte playing the role of Walter Jr. with “such joy and enthusiasm” in an Instagram post. Aaron Paul also paid tribute to the actor at the time of his death on Instagram, saying he’s “so sorry you were hurting my friend. I wish we knew.” As his family, friends and fans continue to mourn the loss of RJ Mitte, we send our condolences.

If you or someone you know is in crisis, we urge you to call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org.

#3580. Are you a warlock tired of being summon-kicked in World of Warcraft: Forever? There's now a mod to fight back with

Being recruited to a World of Warcraft party as a warlock, only to be swiftly kicked again after using your powers to magically summon the party members together in the same place, may soon become a thing of the past. All thanks to a mod made by one especially peeved warlock.

The practice of exploiting warlocks in this way is called summon-kicking, and aside from the in-game reporting feature, there is little recourse to admonish such behavior.

Enter Summoners Union, the add-on mod, which grants the ability to flag and track players who summon-kick thereby building a collective case against them.

The mod was showcased on the World of Warcraft: Forever Reddit by user 274Moons, highlighting its ability to flag players after they boot you from a party, but also that it warns you if anyone in the party has a record of summon-kicking. It can also be combined with an in-game chat channel where warlock comrades can pull together and discuss and ultimately maybe fend off this nasty behavior.

"I play a lock and got tired of the usual 'hey can you summon?', ten minutes at the stone, last person comes through, *You have been removed from the group.*," 274Moons wrote. "So I made an addon about it. It's called The Summoners Union."

According to the add-on's creator, over 500 Warlocks have already downloaded Summon Union. It's a relatively small number in comparison to the wider World of Warcraft: Forever population, but it's a notable start.

"Thank you for this, I hate being just a taxi," wrote user Gregore997. Others also were quick to thank 274Moons for their service to all the Warlocks out there, such as Nangz who wrote: "Please keep the community sharing!".

World of Warcraft: Forever has been out for a little while now and it's been received rather well, breaking records for the series in terms of active players. The playerbase is currently awaiting the release of the game's first raids next month.

It's prickly and keeps you at arms' length, but Queen's Domain is a new all-timer.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Metroidvania is an annoying genre name, but it's useful. A Metroid-type game, with a little 'vania for the fellas: Platform around an open-ended, vertically-oriented world. When you hit a wall, go somewhere else until you unlock a movement-centric powerup to open new pathways. They call 'em "search-action" games in Japan, and that's a way better name.

They're mostly 2D. Metroid Prime did it 3D-style and it's an all-time classic. Dark Souls 1 had the dense, vertical, interconnected world, but not the movement stuff, so let's say it doesn't count as a genre-mate. Queen's Domain is the best game of this style I have ever played, 2D or 3D. Hollow Knight, Symphony of the Night, Metroid Prime⁠—I love 'em, but there's a new queen of the genre. After around 50 hours, four endings, all 52 achievements, and a lot of collectible hunting, I remain in awe of this game.

It's mysterious, prickly, strange, and wonderful. It has writing and story⁠—and what's there is good⁠—but it is a peak "show, don't tell" sort of game. Its more obscure endings demand completion of exacting, Nintendo 64-style collectathons, but almost one in 10 players on Steam have gone to the effort⁠—just over 10% for ending number three, approaching 8% for ending four at the time of writing. That's nuts when you consider the amount of people who buy a game on Steam, noodle around for half an hour, and decide it's not for them or that they'll come back later. But this game has inspired that level of obsession from its players⁠, myself included.

Queen's Domain's lack of guidance and retro style of first person melee combat have not been to all tastes on our team, and its first 30 minutes to an hour of gameplay, while enticing and atmospheric, are its most challenging and frustrating given the absence of a game-defining movement mechanic. I see this as less a flaw, more a question of taste—the contrast between that first half hour and what comes after is crucial. I urge all-comers to dig deep for some good old-fashioned stick-toitiveness and/or use the cheat code for a semi-automatic Soviet battle rifle to get through this section⁠—it weirdly does not kill the immersion.

It feels deranged and impossible that this game was made by two people (not including QA and marketing), and retails for twenty bucks.

You play as a prince searching for his father on a distant archipelago, the elder royal having set out to slay an ancient evil. Knowing the survival rate of protagonists' dads in this line of work, you'll also likely have to slay said evil yourself.

There are tons of fun lore books and notes scattered throughout Queen's Domain, while its supporting NPC cast is lightly-sketched but endearing. This game's best storytelling, though, is environmental: The shared enemy types and statuary in two different zones implying a shared history between them, for example. Or two, seemingly-unrelated areas revealed to be connected by an end-game shortcut you'll only find after dozens of hours, implying an exchange or connection between the two. There is an X-factor of partially-explained fictional history and implied storytelling in Queen's Domain that stands proudly with the likes of Dark Souls or Metroid Prime. Sure, there's "lore," but what's more important is what you interpret and take away from this world.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

And the interconnected world of the Isle of Neasied is a mechanical marvel, one that fits together and makes sense with almost no fudging⁠—co-developer Eric Berger indicated to me in a recent interview that there is a single instance of two zones that would clip into each other slightly if loaded at the same time. That's it.

How many bad or just mediocre 2D metroidvanias are there at this point? Ones with truly excellent worlds, like last year's Hollow Knight: Silksong, are rare triumphs. Managing this magic in full 3D is generationally rare.

Progressing through Queen's Domain for the first time, "Where the hell am I?" "Wait, it keeps going?" and "What even is this game?" were the sorts of things I frequently muttered to myself to my wife's growing concern. There are one-way shortcuts to terrifying, endgame, ball-buster areas hidden in plain sight in the starting zones, a hilarious way to haze careless players reminiscent of the infamous Caelid teleporter chest in Elden Ring. But I love that there was no teleportation required in Queen's Domain, just exploiting the natural way this game's levels fit together like puzzle pieces.

Queen's Domain isn't concerned if players see every cool thing it has to offer, but it has so many moments of serendipitous discovery, this potential for surprise and wonder, you have strong odds of stumbling across at least a few organically. For me, these moments number among my very favorite in the hobby. And this is my favorite part of Queen's Domain, its sense of pure, unadulterated adventure. 49 out of 50 hours in, it still had one more breathtaking thing to show me, a reward for its most gruelling collectathon quest. But if you only have the time or patience to see the first two of four endings on a 25 hour or so critical path, I don't think you'll leave disappointed.

I always remember one critique from the reviews of Metroid Prime I read over the years, and then I felt it, viscerally, when I finally played the game myself: The backtracking. Revisiting old areas with new powers is a foundational part of the metroidvania genre, but it can often make for frustrating busywork. I habitually battle a sense of "what the hell am I supposed to be doing" in these games, or else find it a chore to truck back through areas, looking for the one thing I missed.

Queen's Domain pulls a magic trick in this regard, and meaningfully moves the ball forward for the whole genre. My first time through every area was tense, challenging, and meaningful, but backtracking was easy and fun. The closest it ever got to being a chore was when I had to redo a challenging room in the final dungeon to look for a hidden chest, but that's about it.

Queen's Domain's teleporter economy is a big part of this. There are checkpoint save crystals, as well as teleporter pads connecting the main areas together, with consumable items to warp back to your most recent save crystal and access the teleporter pad network. Early on, these items are rare and highly-prized, useful in an emergency or on completing a zone's critical path. They grow more plentiful as the game goes on, and eventually, you find infinitely reusable versions of them.

It reminds me of Morrowind: You start out trudging everywhere, but eventually Almsivi and Divine Intervention spells, plus the Silt Strider network, let you zoom around like you have access to the best public transit system in the world. The warp pads and save crystals in Queen's Domain are so centrally, strategically located as to make endgame backtracking a breeze.

The other key is Queen's Domain's movement tools, mostly the central airdash mechanic granted in the first level, and slowly expanded upon throughout the game. Those early game areas feel so threatening and vast with access to only one to three airdashes, but at the end of the game, with a full 10 and the [REDACTED] spoilery endgame power? I felt like I was using cheat codes, zooming around the ceilings of levels that gave me so much trouble just hours previously.

It feels like the culmination of the metroidvania exploration and movement promise, the most extreme contrast of early game struggle to endgame mastery I've ever seen in one of these games, and it contributes to a world that's a pleasure to backtrack through, not a chore.

I found the combat in Queen's Domain to be serviceable, but enjoyable in a similar way to Metroid Prime or fellow indie King's Field homage, Lunacid. The melee combat relies on a basic rhythm that can be found everywhere from King's Field, to Ultima Underworld, to The Elder Scrolls: Bait out an enemy's attack while backstepping away, then move in to bop them on the nose. This style of first person melee feels like an old friend to me, but it's admittedly played out.

Queen's Domain spices things up with a particularly satisfying system of throwing weapons, as well as weapon-by-weapon special attacks reminiscent of the ashes of war from Elden Ring. Like in Elden Ring, generic, common weapons have pretty basic⁠—but often reliable⁠—special attacks, while the Legendary Badass Godsword always has some fantasy bullshit that put a smile on my face. The weapon variety picked up a lot of slack for the otherwise "just ok" combat.

Coming back to a point I made at the beginning, this combat, in its most basic form at the very beginning of the game, has been the biggest stumbling block I've seen other players encounter, the filter keeping them from the coolest parts of Queen's Domain. I don't think I would change how Queen's Domain reveals itself, and I don't know how to get more people past that barrier aside from recommending they just grab the damn gun.

I found Queen's Domain to be a polished experience on desktop PC and Steam Deck. I had one crash using photo mode, then another while using a weapon's special attack⁠—I was unable to replicate either. Thankfully, Queen's Domain does keep backup autosaves in addition to checkpoint saves for just such an occasion. Performance and stability have otherwise been rock solid for me, but I will note that Queen's Domain is a bit of a battery hog on Steam Deck. I found a 10-watt TDP limit and 45fps cap to be a sweet spot for two-and-a-half to three hours of uptime on an original LCD model.

These are the largely prosaic concerns nibbling at the edges of a new cult masterpiece. I found Queen's Domain invigorating, a reminder of how surprising and wonderful games can be. I'm going to be thinking about it for years to come, and I will absolutely replay it once I've forgotten enough of it. I cannot wait to see what development duo Bradley Boothe and Eric Berger do next. You owe it to yourself to play this game.

It's prickly and keeps you at arms' length, but Queen's Domain is a new all-timer.

#3577. Union Vote Fails In Landslide At GTA 6 Studio Rockstar Games As 75 Percent Of Devs Vote No

Grand Theft Auto VIGTA 6Rockstar GamesUnion

Rockstar Games will not be forced to formally recognize a union at the Grand Theft Auto 6 studio after its developers based in the UK voted overwhelmingly against the initiative. The weeks-long voting process played out as Rockstar launched the open-world hit to over 30 million sales in its first day.

Voting began on November 12 and concluded today on November 26. Workers at Rockstar Games voted 75 percent against the recognition agreement with the IWGB Game Workers Union. The initiate would have formalized collective bargaining efforts around things like overtime, bonuses, layoffs, and AI. Developers in favor of unionizing can still work with the IGWB, but there will be no regular meetings with management to hash out new policies.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe said in a statement shared with Kotaku. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

The IWGB Game Workers Union pushing the vote released the following statement:

For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society – this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for. Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favor of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.

Whilst we haven’t emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening. People entirely unfamiliar with unions were for the first time debating employment conditions, collective bargaining rights, and our contracts. We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions can lead us.

A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it’s one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We’ll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against AI and layoffs.

The power to shape our working lives has always been, and will always be, in our hands.

The vote comes roughly a year after Rockstar fired dozens of developers it accused of gross misconduct and breaking confidentiality rules around the development of GTA 6. The fired workers accused the studio of union busting, which it has denied, and a legal fight has been ongoing over the last 12 months at a labor tribunal. A final judgement in that case is still pending. As recently as this month, members of both sides of the dispute were testifying on the record for the case.

Florence Pugh is one of the biggest movie stars we have right now. I mean she’s in both films bearing the Dunesday nickname on the 2026 movie schedule for crying out loud! So, I’d expect a director to move mountains in order to get her on their film. It turns out Pugh had balls of steel even before she earned her A-list status. When she was just 22, she was faced with the ultimate Sophie’s Choice of movie roles.

If you were to ask me what two Florence Pugh movies turned her from a burgeoning talent into a one of my favorite actors alive, I’d say it was the one-two punch of her portraying Dani in Midsommar and playing Amy March in Little Women back in 2019. As it happens, those are the same two films that she almost had to pick between. Pugh shared what it took to land both, recently, and I had no idea.

I knew in my gut that I had to do both. And, I knew that if I let one of them go, I would regret that decision for the rest of my life. I called both directors with a big ball of nerves in my stomach because I really wasn’t at the stage of my career where I should be calling a director and telling them that they need to reschedule their shoot, but I did.

This, ladies and gentleman is yet another reason why Florence Pugh is the major name she is. She clearly understood at the time that she had stumbled onto two incredible parts, and she didn't want to choose, despite others telling her she must. With that in mind, she pushed aside any fears and decided to simply ask for what she wanted. Here’s what happened next, per her interview with Elle:

I remember just telling myself like, ‘This is really hard. This is going to require for you to be very brave, but you need to do this because if you don’t you’ll regret not trying.’ And I did, and they made it work. So, I’m grateful for that.

Pugh ended up shooting Midsommar first with writer/director Ari Aster, which proved to be a taxing shoot for the actress. It was all worth it because the A24 film has since become known as one of the best horror movies of all time, with Dani’s May Queen and the Bear also becoming a popular Halloween costume, too. Pugh later also got a Midsommar tattoo to immortalize the movie on her body.

Right after she made Midsommar in Hungary, Pugh ventured to Massachusetts to make Little Women with writer/director Greta Gerwig alongside a cast including Timothée Chalamet, Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Laura Dern and Meryl Streep. Whew, what a list! Little Women went on to give Pugh her first (and still only) Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Actress. Oh, and it also changed how we think about Amy March being a villain in the literary classic, probably forever.

While it feels like the absolute correct order for Pugh to have shot the films, she has spoken about getting depressed after coming home from the leftover Midsommar feelings she had “shelved” when making the joyful book adaptation about sisters.

Pugh's story goes to show, sometimes you just need to ask for what you want, and maybe you’ll get it! It’s particularly a good anecdote for people who might think they need to “earn” the right to request something, when that’s not always the case! And thank goodness she did, because her roles in Midsommar and Little Women are and will always be all-timers for her.

There are so many environmental encounters in GTA 6, I think I'd need months to see them all. It seems NPCs are having loud, obnoxious conversations everywhere I turn, from tips on places to rob to animal rights activists freeing a polar bear in the middle of the highway. Loitering to hear them out comes with the risk of getting entirely sidetracked while out in free roam, so I constantly need to curb my own curiosity. Especially if I want any hope of finishing GTA 6 before Christmas.

But while driving away from the Port Gellhorn motel as Jason one evening, a frantic woman's pleas made me hit the brakes. She's standing beneath a huge billboard at a near deserted intersection, no car in sight, with little more than a bathrobe protecting her modesty. My Jason is a gentleman, so of course I ask her what's wrong. And so began Jason's forays into pensioner BDSM.

The woman thanks Jason profusely and tells her of her troubles: she and her husband were playing a game and now he's unresponsive. I agree to help her out, already wary of the fact that she's wearing thigh-high stockings under that bathrobe.

Entering the bedroom of the couple's stately farmhouse, I see a mostly-naked man dangling from the ceiling. He's not hanging by his neck or anything. He's hogtied in a sex swing. I barely have time to register the person in a scalp-to-toe latex body suit sitting in front of a dog food bowl in the bedroom corner before the woman screeches for me to get her husband down.

I oblige, naturally, nearly drowning in musty old people sweat as the man's bloated stomach bulges against poor Jason's face. He drops the man to the ground, proclaiming him dead – only for the dead man's wife to demand he help her dispose of the body. They're very important people, you see, and she cannot have the scandal of Death by Dominatrix tarnishing their reputation.

I sling the fat old man back over my shoulder and head out into the yard, making for the river at the bottom edge of the property. Just as I'm about to toss him, the man sputters to life. Once he's righted himself, he starts blustering bitterly about how his wife tried to murder him. He said the safe word, after all! Jason doesn't get a chance to respond, and I'm already so deep in this elderly sex scandal that I need to know what happens next.

I follow him back toward the house as he continues to rant about his wife's devious plot, finally confronting her in the kitchen. Why didn't she stop when he gave the safe word, he asks? She tells him off; he was giving the wrong word all along. Things quickly get, uh, uncomfortable; as the woman scolds him for being a filthy little liberal who deserves to be punished. She gestures back into their den of horrors. The newly revived man looks at Jason and cheers wildly, marching merrily back toward the contraption that had very nearly killed him.

Yes, I help him get back into the sex swing. Yes, I have to shake the rubber-suited person off my leg when it tries to lick my shoe. And yes, weirdly, it all was entirely worth it – after getting back to his car, a BuckMe payment for $3,000 pops up on Jason's phone. Could have used a few more zeroes, sure, but at this stage in the game, I'll take all the handouts I can get – especially when no gunshots are required.

#3574. Don't expect a GTA set outside the USA anytime soon, as Rockstar has "not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else"

"There never ceases to be a more interesting place."

Would Rockstar really set a future Grand Theft Auto game outside of the United States? The concept's been mooted recently, particularly in reporting on a recent Rockstar interview with The Guardian, where co-studio head Rob Nelson quipped: "Never say never." But speaking to Eurogamer in another interview since then, I would say it's unlikely.

During our conversation, I asked Nelson about the choice of the US as an ongoing setting for the games, and what in particular drove Rockstar's continuing infatuation with the country across both GTA and Red Dead Redemption.

"I don't know," Nelson said initially. "It's just that there never ceases to be a more interesting place to think about setting it. I just think that it's constantly changing, there's constantly stuff for us to respond to, and it works from a gameplay standpoint in terms of what we want to do."

A little more conclusively, he added: "We have not had a lot of conversations over doing it anywhere else."

That doesn't quite settle it for good, of course. Nelson's "never say never" comments still stand, but coupled with his follow-up response to The Guardian, where he noted "there's still so much to do in America," it seems we can pretty confidently pin the next GTA's location as somewhere, once again, within the United States.

I also wouldn't be surprised if there were early ideas as to where exactly within the US the next GTA might end up. The decision on Florida was one of the earliest Rockstar made this time, for instance. As Nelson explained to me, with GTA 6: "You first decide on place, for GTA – where are we going to set it?"

That was "quick", this time, he noted. "We had three major cities established, this was the one that we hadn't been back to recently. It's also felt [amongst the team]: if you want to reflect something about contemporary America, Florida is a pretty good place to give you a wide range of craziness, and sort of variety in terms of experience."

That then led to early research trips to Florida, Nelson explained, which in turn informed the game's characters and mechanics – including the more interactive, thoughtful, empathetic world Nelson also explained to me, and the decision around the big character moment in the early minutes of the game's prologue.

For much more on GTA 6's setting, meanwhile, our full GTA 6 map and extensive GTA 6 walkthrough might come in handy. And all this said, frankly, I'm more than happy to stay here in Leonida for some time - as was probably made quite clear in our five-star GTA 6 review.

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally out, and it made more money than Taylor Swift's Eras Tour. Now, one of its lead actors is getting candid about it all. The voice of Lucia, Manni L. Perez, has spoken out following the game's release about how her life has been "such a whirlwind" since launch day.

Perez's Lucia has been a big topic of discussion over the past week, as couples joke that their partner is cheating on them with her. She didn't have anything to say about that, as it seems like she's just now catching her breath and sharing gratitude on Instagram to the fans that helped make the game's release bigger than any show on the 2026 TV schedule:

Life has been such a whirlwind these past couple of days and I just want to take a moment to say thank you. Thank you to all the new followers and the positive reception the game and my character have received. I've dedicated almost a decade bringing Lucia to life. She's been such a significant part of mine and I am beyond grateful she now gets to be a small part of yours.

Clearly, she's very thankful for all of this, which is fitting considering it was just Thanksgiving. And she's deserving of the praise too, considering how well-received the game already is and how great she is in it.

I guess I shouldn't be surprised that Manni Perez looks a lot like Lucia, as Grand Theft Auto does like to model its characters after the voice actors who play them. Still, even well-known celebrities can look a little different in the game, whereas Perez looks like she could star in a future movie about Jason and Lucia. It would be awesome if she were considered for the role if there are discussions!

William Shatner Clarifies His Stance On Grand Theft Auto VI After Backlash

It's wild to think about, and I love how humble Manni Perez is in her thanks. No joke, I would guess there are as many people listening to her voice in the game as there are who saw some of the biggest releases on the 2026 movie schedule. It's good to see her be so humble about it all, and she has nothing but gratitude to everyone enjoying the game.

Lucia and Jason are a hot topic after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, as they buck the usual trend of what we've seen from previous games in this franchise. Previous entries haven't had existing relationships for players to maintain, and I wouldn't say the protagonists were necessarily anyone the player felt compelled to root for.

Lucia is also the first female protagonist of Grand Theft Auto, as players can opt to swap between the two in order to complete missions. While there was some initial backlash to the game making such a radical change, it appears that the people are more in support of the decision than against it.

Grand Theft Auto VI is available to purchase right now, and a great buy for those looking for something to spend the rest of the year obsessed with. I've spent a couple of hours in the game just listening to the various radio stations in my car, and can't wait to see what other stuff unlocks the longer I play it!

When Hitman 3 first launched in 2021, it was the first time since Absolution that I'd felt a strong urge to step into the shoes of Agent 47. The reason: its Berlin level. Set in the grimy, sweaty Club Hölle, it was the first time I'd ever seen a videogame get a nightclub right. The density of people on the dancefloor, the slight griminess that coated the whole place. The lights, the music. I didn't think another game would out-do it anytime soon.

There's an awful lot to be impressed with in Rockstar's newest blockbuster—and I should hope so, considering how much money and time went into making the damn thing—but nothing has stood out to me more than Leonida's nightlife. Hitman 3 did it excellently in isolation, but GTA 6 has managed to incorporate an immersive, lively club scene right into the open world.

And after spending far too much time in Vice City's Big Three—that's NINE1NINE, Jack of Hearts, and The Vault—I'm floored not only by how good a job Rockstar did of making them feel like a club you would end up inside in real life, but how distinct they all are from one another.

You've got your overpriced luxury half-strip-club, half-regular-club with NINE1NINE (inspired by Miami's own E11EVEN), where a beer costs 15 goddamn bucks even after you already fork out the $150 cover charge to get in. There's the sticky, dollar bill-laden floors of Jack of Hearts where MCs belt out over the mic and the bass practically splits the speakers open. And then you've got the cool, underground rave vibes of The Vault with multiple floors offering different music styles.

Even before heading inside each one, its patrons spill out of the doors and onto the sidewalks. Some are queueing up waiting to get in, while others huddle around back entrances having a smoke and talking about all the diabolical topics you get into after a few drinks. They aren't just isolated interiors, capturing the parts of the night that happen outside of the club itself.

That's an issue videogame nightclubs so often have: its people. A smattering of NPCs here and there, standing idly around in a venue that's a little too well-lit and making me feel like I just rocked up at 2 pm on a Monday afternoon.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Yet everywhere you look in GTA 6's nightclubs, you'll find swarms of bodies. The Vault is by far my favourite nightclub of the three—perhaps because it's the closest to what I've experienced in the real world—and as I walked around it shocked me just how carefully placed every single person felt.

The dancefloor is densely packed and I have to weave through sweaty bodies to make my way to the front. That's already impressive enough in itself. But it's also the punters who clutter the stairways; some sat on a step alone as they scroll through their phone, others gathered in clusters in an attempt to converse away from the noise and throng of drunken ravers. I've seen those people countless times in my own real-life nighttime excursions. Hell, I've been those people.

Sure, these people are ultimately set pieces, rarely (if ever) moving from their carefully curated posts. Dancers might wander around and bartenders will walk up and down serving drinks, leaving the rest of its people surprisingly static. But in the grand scheme of things, it doesn't matter. How often are you paying attention to what everyone else is up to in a nightclub, anyway?

Even the ways these things are decorated, man. Seeing half-drunk beer bottles perched atop ATM machines and drink cups cluttering up the bar makes me feel like people have actually been here and lived their life. There are so many small details that have gone into making each place feel like somewhere you've been in the real world, and that's even without me mentioning all the extra little ways Sony's DualSense controller amps up the experience.

I'm not sure how long it'll be until we get nightclubs that feel this damn good again. They feel like venues put together by people who've stayed out dancing until the lights come on at 3 am, only filtered out onto the streets by harsh fluorescents and the sudden absence of music. From the music choices, to the strobed lights and fog machines, to those utterly wild conversations you'd only be privy to in the smoking area, Rockstar has managed to curate the best nightlife going.
