#3525. WoW: Forever’s Best Buffs Now Work As Intended

World of Warcraft: Forever players will now be able to get even more benefit from the game's strongest buffs, as developer Blizzard's latest hotfix has made World Buffs persist across loading screens as intended.

World Buffs are powerful stat-boosting effects granted to players in a particular area for certain events. The most common World Buff players see is Warchief's Blessing on the Horde and the new Might of Stormwind for the Alliance, which are granted to all players in Orgrimmar, Stormwind, and their surrounding low-level zones when players on their respective faction turn in a specific high-level quest.

Now that players are reaching endgame and turning in the required quest, these buffs are popping off constantly. They grant a whopping 300 hit points, 15% melee haste, and 10 mana regen per five seconds for one hour. At lower levels, those are some serious stats, particularly the 300 HP.

Unfortunately, players haven't been able to take full advantage of the buffs, as a bug was causing them to be lost when hitting a loading screen. That meant any time a group stepped into a dungeon or took a boat or zeppelin to a new location, their World Buffs would be removed.

That has finally been fixed in the latest update, so players can now enter dungeons with World Buffs to help maximize their damage and health. This should be particularly useful for doing dungeons at a slightly lower level than is intended, as the extra HP and melee haste is definitely noticable.

Blizzard clarified in the patch notes that World Buffs will still be removed when entering raids, so players won't be able to stack as many World Buffs as possible before raid night, as was the case in previous versions of classic WoW. 

Other changes found in the patch notes include a fix for an Uldaman boss that players were exploiting to make fast gold. Another is a fix for "a few spells and abilities" that were causing more weapon-proc effects than intended, likely nerfing the DPS of whatever classes were taking advantage of the bug. You can read the full patch notes below.

Blizzard recently outlined in the latest episode of the WoW: Forever podcast how it wants to get rid of the idea of "best-in-slot gear," as well as how the game's has overhauled old-school WoW's player-vs.-player systems. In other Forever news, the game's launch has seen more than 15 million characters created so far, with the highest weekly player numbers for WoW in 15 years. 

WoW: Forever November 23 Hotfix Patch Notes

Classes

  • Druid
    • The 4-piece Feralheart set for Druids now correctly grants 4 Energy regeneration every 1 second for 5 seconds.
  • Priest
    • Mind Vision should no longer proc effects.
    • Shadow
      • Fixed an issue where Dark Inspiration was not granting the correct amount of %Spirit increase if Mind Flay was used to activate it.
      • Fixed an issue where Chastise was not usable in Shadowform.
  • Warlock
    • Destruction
      • Fixed an issue where Intensity was not working on Incinerate.
  • Warrior
    • Fixed an issue where players could have and use Mortal Strike from their spellbook, even without the Mortal Strike talent. This does not remove it from their spellbook but prevents it from being used without the talent point spent.

Dungeons

  • Uldaman
    • The Obsidian Sentinel drops loot as intended.

Items

  • The Filcher’s Cowl no longer has a level requirement.

Professions

  • Cooking
    • Boiled Clams, Clam Chowder, Goblin Deviled Clams, Giant Clam Scorcho, Undermine Clam Chowder, and Clam Linguine each now offer the correct Well Fed bonuses and have been recategorized in the recipe list under “Stamina Food”.
    • Murloc Fin Soup has had its recovery and Well-Fed amounts increased to the next tier of food, bringing it closer to other food of that level.
  • Engineering
    • Fixed a bug that caused Goblin Engineer’s Renewal Gift and Gnome Engineer’s Renewal Gift to appear as broken, unusable question marks in the inventory.
    • Fixed a bug that prevented “The Mortar: Reloaded” recipe from being learned upon learning the “Goblin Mortar” recipe.
  • Leatherworking
    • Fixed a bug that prevented Pattern: Centaur Hoofwarmers from being learnable.

Quests

  • Riverglades - Dunston Willis once again runs near the end of the escort “Dunston Checks Out.”
  • Wetlands - After further study, the quest “For Further Study” now has rewards.
  • Wetlands - The quest “Uncovering the Past” now rewards Ironforge reputation.
  • Wetlands - The quest “Gleaning Our Future” now rewards Ironforge reputation.

Races

  • Fixed an issue where Wisp Form could be applied to players while they were alive.

Spells

  • Fixed an issue where a few spells and abilities were causing more weapon procs than intended.
  • Fixed an issue where World Buffs would fall off when changing areas. They will still fall off when entering raid instances.
  • Fixed an issue where Fengus’ Ferocity was granting twice as much Spell Power as intended.
  • Fixed an issue where Darkmoon Faire buffs were granting twice as much power as intended.

#3523. Sotheby’s Sold the World’s Most Expensive Van Gogh for $190 Million

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in New York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred said the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”

— For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

— Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

— The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

He starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.

Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.

Why is name-dropping important? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?

The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I said, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?

We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.

Chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I said, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.

True Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.

Shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.

I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.

He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.

Chow: Andy said, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”

Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.

The works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.

Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.

“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.

If there’s one big day to circle on what’s left of the 2026 movie schedule, it’s Dunesday. It’s the Friday before Christmas when both Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three are hitting theaters. It’s going to be a huge weekend for the movie business regardless, but the writer and director of Dune 3, Denis Villeneuve, just shared his thoughts on it, and he’s not happy. However, does he have the right to be? Let’s break it down.

First, what exactly did the Dune filmmaker say about Dunesday? In a new interview with Time, the director, who’s completing the trilogy with Part Three, didn’t hold back, saying this:

Listen, I will be honest. The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, 'Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.' Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.

As he points to, the first Dune came out in October 2021 at a time when theaters were still struggling in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite this, the movie made $410.7 million worldwide against a budget of $165 million. Then, the 2024 sequel did even better with a $714.9 million global haul, but that was after it had to be pushed back due to the 2023 Hollywood strikes.

Going into Dune 3, Villeneuve thought the franchise’s struggles would be over, but then Avengers: Doomsday moved its release date to open next to it. The director also said this:

So I was deeply disappointed. But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.

While the paired billing of Barbie and Oppenheimer back in 2023 famously helped both films become meteoric successes at the box office, Villeneuve doesn’t have that point of view for Dunesday. The Avengers films have been known to break huge records, and sharing the date with the latest of them has left him “praying to the gods of cinema” for his own epic.

So, what do the latest numbers say about Dunesday with December 18 just three weeks away? According to the most current projection of $270 million, Avengers: Doomsday already has the highest box office projection the National Research Group has ever recorded (via Deadline). Yes, even higher than Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which recently broke Endgame’s domestic opening weekend record over the summer.

Dune: Part 3, on the other hand, is tracking at around $75 million, with projections suggesting it “wouldn’t be shocking” if it passes $80 million. That would be on par with the previous Dune movie and double the debut earnings of the first film. Plus, as Villeneuve noted, Dune: Part 3 could contribute to one of the biggest box office openings of all time.

So, clearly Dune is not topping Avengers: Doomsday. The big con here is Doomsday is definitely robbing the final Dune film of a No. 1 slot at the box office. However, as the director said, he’s not expecting Avengers numbers for his own film. The other thing to keep in mind is some fans of both franchises might pick Doomsday over Dune. But, let's be real here, I'd assume most fans of both are going to see both in theaters opening weekend some way, somehow! We'll have to wait and see if Doomsday boosts Dune sales, but either way, both movies aren't expected to flop; Doomsday is just a behemoth of a movie impossible to compete against.

On the plus side, Dune could very well become the highest-grossing movie of the series, and wouldn’t it be cool if it cracks $1 billion? We’ll be watching closely this holiday season as the box office for both films shakes out starting December 18.

#3519. Just Like GTA 6, The Witcher 4 Has A PlayStation Deal

CD Projekt Red has announced that just today, November 24, the Polish studio signed new deals with Sony Interactive Entertainment for The Witcher 4's upcoming marketing campaign, among other efforts.

CFO Piotr Nielubowicz told investors that the deals cover CD Projekt Red's games on PlayStation and in the PlayStation Plus catalog, as well as "our collaboration during the upcoming Witcher 4 marketing campaign."

“This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook in this and future years," he said, according to VGC.

No specifics were made available, but the partnership for The Witcher 4's marketing campaign has people theorizing that it could be similar to Rockstar's co-marketing deal with Sony for GTA 6.

Under that agreement, GTA 6 was marketed as a game that "plays best on PS5," even if the jury is out on that being true. Sony also created special GTA 6 DualSense controllers and even custom consoles for NBA players. The PlayStation branding was prioritized over Xbox to give people the impression that they should get it on PlayStation.

The Witcher 4 is in the works now and is expected to launch in 2028 for console and PC. The game kicks off a new trilogy of The Witcher games, which will also include The Witcher 5 and The Witcher 6. These will all be released within a six-year window, so the whole new trilogy could be out by 2034.

The studio is “targeting” a 2028 release for The Witcher 4, so it could be delayed like The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 were before it.

#3518. Call Of Duty’s 19-Year Sales Streak Continues

Circana has released its latest monthly sales report for the US video game industry, and in terms of game sales, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 led the way.

It was the No. 1 best-selling game of October 2026, and that's notable because it marked the 19th consecutive year that a new Call of Duty game has been the top-selling title for its launch month.

This streak began in November 2008 when Call of Duty: World at War beat out Guitar Hero: World Tour and Gears of War 2 to rank No. 1.

Circana also announced that spending on content for consoles dropped by 18% compared to October 2026. It was always going to be a tough comparison, though, as October 2025 saw the releases of Battlefield 6 and Pokemon Legends Z-A.

#3517. William Shatner Reacts to Director John Carpenter's 'Piece of S***' Jab

William Shatner has broken his silence after director John Carpenter called him a “piece of s***” following Shatner’s alleged slight during their first meeting.

“I live in infamy due to the fact that I didn’t look up when you said hello to me,” Shatner, 95, wrote via an Instagram statement on Friday, November 27. “I don’t know why I didn’t look up, but obviously I didn’t hear you.”

The Star Trek actor cheekily added, “I was probably reading a great review of one of your movies and it occupied my attention to the point where I didn’t look up.”

Shatner was referring to Carpenter’s recent claim that he ignored him completely when the Halloween director, 78, attempted to introduce himself at a convention in Orlando, Florida.

“This guy, he’s sitting in the greenroom, on his phone like this [scrolling]. And I just thought, ‘Well, I’m going to go in and introduce myself,’”, Carpenter recalled during a November 18 appearance on the “Dropping Names” podcast. “I said, ‘Hello, Mr. Shatner, I’m John Carpenter.’”

According to Carpenter, Shatner stared at his phone and simply said, “pleasure,” but didn’t “look up from the phone.”

“This piece of s*** did not look up from the phone … He’s an a**hole,” Carpenter declared following the alleged incident.

Shatner addressed the allegations in his statement, claiming, “I would have looked up because you are obviously one of the great directors in film and I admire you so much, and I would’ve relished the chance to talk to you.”

The Miss Congeniality actor insisted that the “next time you see me, please come over and introduce yourself, because I really don’t know what you look like and apparently you know what I look like.”

Shatner added, “But I would enjoy saying hello to you, and this piece of s*** would confide in you his admiration.”

He concluded by writing, “My Best, William Shatner.”

In the caption of the social media statement, Shatner tagged Carpenter and implored him to read the full message. “Love, Bill,” the TV star added.

Hours later, Carpenter responded to Shatner’s message by posting his own Instagram statement addressed to the Boston Legal alum, seemingly burying the hatchet.

“I met you in Orlando, or I should say, I said hello to you and introduced myself in Orlando. You would not look me in the eye. Maybe it’s a Canadian thing,” Carpenter wrote on Friday. “I’m willing to give you another chance. I’m nothing if not generous.”

The filmmaker continued, “Regardless, the next time I see you at a convention, I will happily introduce myself again, and we can actually start our relationship.”

Carpenter concluded with a nod to Shatner’s iconic Star Trek character, writing, “After all, even Captain Kirk deserves a second chance at first contact.”

#3516. Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

When my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside New York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

But what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

“Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”

This is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

To Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”

Over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she says. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”

“There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” says Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and New York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”

He recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell says. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

Gil Schafer, a New York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he says, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”

Nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins says, offering me an issue of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this big apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”

When Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to New Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she says. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

One of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he says, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”

At the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a new one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of big moves,” she says. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger says. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”

Nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she says. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”

PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer says of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”

On average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build new structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning says of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Patience is a big part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer says. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”

People joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”

“I do love them,” Nevins says of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I said, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Currently her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”

Nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she says. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”

In another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The New York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we said to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he says. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”

In the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby said that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”

The Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler says. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”

#3515. The Witcher 4 Wants To Be The GTA 6 Of The Witcher Franchise

There's been a massive gap between new entries in The Witcher series, and for The Witcher 4, developer CD Projekt Red aims to make it the GTA 6 of the series, with a noticeable leap in quality. In its Q3 earnings call, the studio says it has been inspired by the technological and gameplay advancements Rockstar Games has made with GTA 6--especially when compared to 2013's GTA 5--and hopes players will feel the same way when they jump into The Witcher 4.

"First of all, obviously this is a call about us, not about Rockstar," CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski (via Eurogamer). "But I do understand the connection here. Having said that, I'm not going to make a deep-dive and a full-blown review of GTA 5 versus GTA 6. But of course we did look at the game; we did see the differences. We believe there's going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4--I think so, yes. It's been 11 years; we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4."

When The Witcher 3: The Wild Hunt was first released in 2015, it was hailed for raising the bar for open-world adventure games. Its side-quests were singled out for being narratively dense, full of micro-consequences, and on par with the main campaign missions. In the years since, numerous open-world games have used The Witcher 3 as a blueprint, with notable examples being the Assassin's Creed trilogy of Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla alongside Sony's Horizon Zero Dawn and Ghost of Tsushima.

Eleven years later, that bar has been raised again with GTA 6, which offers emergent, player-driven open-world chaos through multiple systems. The world of The Witcher is naturally very different from the consumerism-focused setting of GTA 6, but if The Witcher 4 builds on its predecessor's strengths and adds more nuance to those gameplay mechanics, we could be in for something special.

CDPR also said it's trying to make The Witcher 4 more appealing to mainstream audiences, but it hasn't detailed exactly how it plans to do that. "Our games are different, and they require a certain different approach--we just do things differently than they do. But in terms of the ultimate effect, in terms of breaking out to the mass market awareness: This is for sure something we consider pivotal to whatever we're going to do with our marketing campaigns in the future," Nowakowski said.

Currently, over 500 people are working on The Witcher 4, and CDPR has signed a marketing agreement with PlayStation for the game ahead of its targeted 2028 release. The studio is also chipping away at Cyberpunk 2, but after the launch of GTA 6, the game's creative director joked about canceling it, saying Rockstar's game set a high standard for open-world games.

The cast of Jumanji has been busy promoting their Open World, but their latest video takes the cranberry sauce for most unique. Channeling that dysfunctional family energy we know and love, they gave fans a peek at how they celebrated Thanksgiving with a video of Kevin Hart (hilariously) throwing a temper tantrum.

In what can only be described as proof that these stars are absolute maniacs even off set, the video invites you to celebrate the holidays by going to see Jumanji: Open World when it hits the 2026 movie schedule on Christmas Day. During the video, Dwayne Johnson, Karen Gillan, and Jack Black set out to enjoy a peaceful dinner. However, that’s not what happened when Hart arrived, wondering where his invite to the “very Jumanji Thanksgiving” was. What followed was a truly top-tier crash out. The video was posted on all four of their Instagrams and can be watched below:

A post shared by Dwayne Johnson (@therock)

If you need a minute after that, I understand. I laughed so hard that I immediately had to share the video with my sister. That's because not only did we see them at their comedic best, but it takes Johnson’s classic trolling of his buddy to the next level with a blow-up that brings up ancient history (from 2019). That’s right. The Rock brought up THAT Halloween moment when Hart dressed up as him from the ‘80s, complete with a turtleneck, wig, and a fanny pack. However, for the Moana actor, the fanny pack was a step too far, and he made sure his friend knew it.

Now, the crash out began with a (possible) misunderstanding, as Hart showed up to find his three co-stars eating “a bunch of dishes” they know he likes to eat. The drama took a very soap-inspired turn with Hart pointing out the different foods and discovering even “fake Nick Jonas” got an invite. However, Black gave a fun nod to Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle by making it clear: “Fake Nick Jonas is with me.” Thankfully, I’m not the only one laughing, as people can’t get enough of these four:

These are just some of fans’ favorite moments in the video. Clearly, they came ready to deliver the comedy goods, from Hart accusing them of “eating like a bunch of heathens” to coughing on the food. However, his tantrum feels like a nod to one of his performances as Lil’ Toot Toot in the newest trailer.

Now, while Johnson and Hart fighting and Jack Black being so casual were obvious delights of this new video, it was seeing Karen Gillan in mom-mode that was a favorite. Plus, this is a hilarious reminder of the zany antics she dealt with (or caused) on set.

Overall, Black said it best: “This is what Thanksgiving is all about: dysfunction, drama, that’s Thanksgiving.” By the end of the video, not only was everything resolved, but the cast had successfully welcomed us back to the jungle. Though am I the only one who desperately wants to see a ‘mock’ reality TV show with these four, and of course, fake Nick Jonas?

This may be the closest we get to that dream, but we will see the four reunite with the real Nick Jonas on Christmas Day. In the meantime, you can rewatch every insane moment from the first two Jumanji movies with a Hulu subscription.

#3513. GTA 6 Modders Are Trying To Vibe-Code A PC Port, And It’s Not Going Well

PC modders are racing to get GTA 6 playable on PC after the leak of the game's complete Xbox build, but so far it doesn't look too promising.

GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive and developer Rockstar Games haven't been sitting idle either, as one of the leads behind the Project Leonida Discord group claimed in now-deleted social media posts that they were stepping away from the mammoth task of getting GTA 6 to run on PC. Project Leonida has also been taken down, but it's not the only group trying to get GTA 6 running outside of PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

None of these groups have succeeded yet, and as Twitter user Chasm detailed online, maybe relying heavily on AI tools isn't the way to go. Dev streams have been full of users leveraging generative AI tools to do something, with several prompts being absolute gems of wishful thinking. Here's a snippet of what people have been throwing at Google's Antigravity, while butchering the English language:

  • Continue working and do apply ever part of the code
  • make no mistakes
  • You need todo one thing at a time not a little bit of everything
  • we need all the game start like the rockstar launch so on that stuff, not in game stuff yet
  • work faster
  • there has to be a faster way to iterate than this

Even with an army of enthusiasts throwing prompts and cash at generative AI, a copied version of GTA 6 still seems far out of reach. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick commented in March that the idea of using AI and simply pushing a button to make a hit game was "laughable," and he referenced the music industry, which is grappling with a flood of AI slop to top streaming platforms. "Right now [in music] there are programs that allow you to put out a prompt and get a professionally recorded song spit back out at you. It sounds like a song, but I defy you to listen to it more than once. It's great to send as a greeting card to your partner on their birthday, but that's about it," Zelnick said.

Whatever progress is made in the GTA 6 PC port scene, don't expect it to last long before Take-Two's lawyers pounce. The publisher hasn't shied away from protecting its IP in the past, and takedown notices for any future GTA 6-related projects seem likely. In related GTA 6 news, you can read up on how the game has given Pornhub a hard time and how it became the biggest launch in PlayStation history.

#3512. Welcome to Plathville’s Ken Palmer Confirms He and Kim Plath Have Split

Welcome to Plathville’s Ken Palmer has confirmed that he and Kim Plath are no longer an item.

Palmer posted a carousel of outdoorsy photos via his Instagram on Wednesday, November 25, announcing, “I’m officially a Mississippian again.”

The post prompted his followers to question whether the move meant that he and Plath had gone their separate ways.

Palmer confirmed the split in the comments section. When one commenter suggested that Ken walked away due to Kim’s weight — which he had previously described on the show as a “dealbreaker” if she didn’t shed pounds — he claimed that it wasn’t the only reason for the breakup.

“Weight, laziness, and hygiene issues all go hand in hand. Don’t judge me. She put on 130 pounds in 4 years,” he wrote. “I’ve forgiven her twice before for hooking up with other men too.”

After Ken posted a photo of himself with his cat via Instagram the following day, he also confirmed there was no argument before they called time on their relationship.

“So did you and Kim have a fight? You seemed so in love,” asked a follower. Ken replied, “Irreconcilable differences. No fight.”

For her part, Kim has not yet commented publicly on the split.

Kim had been dating Ken since 2022, following her split from ex-husband Barry Plath. The exes share nine children: Ethan, Hosanna, Micah, Moriah, Lydia, Isaac, Amber, Cassia and Mercy. Their 10th child, son Joshua, died in 2008 when he was 17 months old following a farm accident.

Kim and Ken have broken up and reconciled several times in the past.

In May 2026, their relationship issues were shown on an episode of Welcome to Plathville when Ken called out Kim for not putting in enough effort to lose weight.

“I want her to be around for a long time for me and for the kids,” Ken told the cameras in the May 19 episode of the TLC series. “But I feel like she just kind of put the getting healthy [plan] on the back burner.”

He added, “I’m not seeing any changes and it’s starting to get frustrating.”

In the episode, Kim opened up to Ken about the issues she’s having when it comes to her weight loss journey.

“It’s been a little bit daunting, you know, being in my 50s and trying to lose weight. I mean, it’s not as easy as it was in my 20s or even in my 30s,” Kim told Ken as they sat on a swing on their farm. “I’m trying to work out more and I don’t know. There’s days where it’s just really hard to work in something, you know?”

Ken was seemingly unconvinced that Kim was trying hard enough to take care of herself and admitted it was a sticking point for him.

“I really love Kim and I want to see her get healthier, but I think it could potentially be a deal breaker if she is not going to commit to her health,” Ken said in a confessional. “It makes me wonder, is she committed to me?”

Ken’s comments left Kim concerned. In a confessional, Kim said she felt pressured to lose weight or lose the relationship.

“I don’t really like that it’s a deal breaker for him. I mean, I feel like he’s giving me an ultimatum,” she said at the time. “I do worry about the future of our relationship when I hear him say things like that.”

#3511. From a gown purchased with wartime rations to a secret engraving on the ring: Inside the historic royal wedding of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip

Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding

The Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was said to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

In 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately said yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.

Princess Elizabeth with Philip Mountbatten on their wedding day

The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

Like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

Designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

Princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

As Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”

Princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, said to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

All royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.

Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.

The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.

The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.

Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.

The wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip walking down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, followed by their bridesmaids and pages

There were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

Together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.)

The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”

The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

On the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.

The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.

During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.

The couple waving from the balcony of Buckingham Palace

Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

Although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.

Mr Schur, chief confectioner at McVitie and Price, putting the final touches to the wedding cake

The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

Over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.

The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip being showered with rose petals as they leave Buckingham Palace, London, for their honeymoon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sure, Full House premiered nearly 40 years ago, but that doesn’t mean Candace Cameron Bure isn’t still getting residual payments from her time in one of the most well-adjusted sitcom families. No matter how extensive her previous Hallmark catalog is or how many movies she makes heading the Great American Family network, she will always be remembered as D.J. Tanner from the beloved comedy series and its Netflix TV revival, Fuller House. According to the sitcom star, the checks she still gets reflect that.

Even though most actors never talk about the size of their paychecks, Jodie Sweetin made headlines earlier this year when she revealed that she had received just one cent from the popular sitcom. Bure very clearly set the record straight that that’s not the experience she’s had. During her recent appearance on The McBride Rewind podcast, she pointed out how “substantial” her own checks still are. She said:

I actually saw that, and she said she doesn’t get much now. I was like, ‘Jodie, you got to check with your agent or you got to call your bank ‘cause I still get residuals.'

Stories about actors receiving tiny residual checks is nothing new. Abbott Elementary’s William Stanford Davis showed off his 5-cent check and Mandy Moore opened up about making 81 cents for This Is Us. Bure herself even admitted receiving tons of $6 and $7 residuals for past commercials, voice-over work, and other projects she’s done over the years. What really stands out when it comes to Full House is the big gap that seemingly exists between two members of the same sitcom family.

There’s no way to know whether the difference in residual checks could have something to do with the contracts Candace Cameron Bure and Jodie Sweetin signed at the time, or if something else is going on, but there clearly is a difference in the money the co-stars are receiving. Along with her suggestion to check with her agent or call her bank, Bure stressed:

Yeah, no… The checks for Full House are still substantial. I’m always happy when I open my check up and deposit it.

Although it's really none of my business, I'm now so curious about just how big the difference in these residual checks really is. Without giving the exact specifics, it seems Bure is receiving considerably more than the one cent her Tanner sister is receiving. This isn’t just a one-off, as Bure said that she continues to receive these checks regularly.

While there was no specific streaming deal made with the actors at the time of the original series, since that didn’t actually exist yet, Bure said she still receives a percentage of the deals made to keep Full House available to viewers even if she’s not getting paid per stream. I’ll absolutely admit to not knowing the ins and outs of what goes into residual deals for cast members, but that definitely sounds like Jodie Sweetin should be making more than one cent.

You can currently stream the ABC sitcom with your Hulu subscription and your Disney+ subscription.

#3508. WWE's Bronson Reed Dead at 38, Leaves Behind Pregnant Wife and Daughter

WWE star Bronson Reed has died after suffering an injury during an event in Saudi Arabia earlier this month.

Reed (real name Jermaine Haley) died on Friday, November 27, due to “medical complications,” WWE announced. He was 38.

“Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague,” the company said in a statement on Friday. “Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans.”

Reed reportedly suffered broken ribs and a lacerated kidney at WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on November 7, after being thrown off the stage by Oba Femi and crashing through tables.

The pro wrestler traveled back home to the United States after undergoing surgery in Saudi Arabia earlier this month, The Wrestling Observer reported on November 17.

WWE held a traditional ten-bell salute before their live event in Atlanta on Friday night in Reed’s honor.

Reed’s shocking death sent reverberations throughout the pro wrestling community.

“I can’t believe this is real,” WWE reporter Jackie Redmond wrote via X. “Bronson was an amazing person. Incredibly kind. I am devastated for his young family. My thoughts and prayers go out to those closest to him and everyone that loved him. It’s not fair.”

TNA Wrestling’s Bear Bronson shared, “Brutally heartbreaking. Jermaine was a massive inspiration to so many & such a genuinely kind human being. RIP Bronson Reed 💔 My thoughts are with his family & all of his close ones at this time.”

“Love you brother,” WWE’s Grayson Waller said. “Thank you for opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”

WWE’s Brooks Jensen shared, “Really heartbreaking to hear about this…Bronson was a great human being who you could tell loved what he did and I’ll never forget sharing conversations about Japanese wrestling … We lost not only a great pro wrestler but an incredible human being.”

TNA Wrestling’s Ash by Elegance, who formerly wrestled in WWE as Dana Brooke wrote, “My heart is just broken 💔 … another legend gone too soon! Bronson was ALWAYSSSS so so kind & just the most polite person… his wife was an absolute blessing talking with many times while coping with somethings.. Heaven received another Angel!!!”

“A few years ago, I had a brief interaction with Bronson Reed, and it’s a moment I remember,” WWE Hall of Famer Ricky Morton shared. “He had asked for advice. This business brings a lot of people into your life, and you never know how much a small interaction can mean. So heartbreaking. Life is so precious.”

#3507. Witcher 4 Won’t Be A PS5 Exclusive After New Deal With PlayStation

CD Projekt Red and Sony Interactive Entertainment just announced a marketing deal for The Witcher 4, but that doesn't mean the game will be exclusive to PlayStation.

CD Projekt Red's Michał Nowakowski said on social media, "Just to be clear: The Witcher 4 and our other upcoming titles will remain multiplatform."

The marketing deal could be similar to the one between Rockstar and Sony for GTA 6, where GTA 6 was given preferential treatment on PS5 in a number of ways in the marketing campaign.

Beyond The Witcher 4, CD Projekt Red is making Cyberpunk 2, a new IP codenamed Hadar, a new game believed to be a multiplayer The Witcher title, and a remake of the original Witcher. On the mobile side, CD Projekt Red is working with Scopely on a new game that hasn't been announced yet.

The Witcher 4 now has more than 500 people working on it, and the game is expected to release in 2028. Given that timing, The Witcher 4 likely won't be on a disc because Sony won't support game discs beginning in January 2028.

That being said, CD Projekt Red is promising that The Witcher 4 will have some kind of physical goodies for fans.

In other news about The Witcher 4, CD Projekt Red recently discussed the game in comparison to GTA 6.

"Of course we did look at the game; we did see the differences. We believe there’s going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4–I think so, yes," Nowakowski said. "It’s been 11 years; we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4.”

#3506. Who Will Be The Next Bond Girl?

Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

The exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

Léa Seydoux and Daniel Craig pose as they arrive on the set of No Time To Die on September 09, 2019 in Matera, Italy.

In a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she said with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”

When pressed on who Pattinson's female lead might be, Seydoux expressed mixed feelings about the British spy's latest iteration. With the purchase of the Bond IP by Amazon, “It became American," Seydoux said. “But I’m sure the movie will be great because it’s directed by Denis Villeneuve, who’s a very talented director. I’m sure he will do something great.”

The online megamart took control of the storied franchise in 2023, after which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos controversially sought feedback on the title character's casting via X. The announcement of Villeneuve as the next film's director brought things back from the brink.

Bezos, who confirmed that he was “very involved” in the film's casting process, also seems to give Seydoux pause. In an interview with Variety, she admitted “was a bit sad when I heard that it was sold (…) but now that it’s Denis, I was like, Oh, at least it’s him, so it will be cinema.”

Denis Villeneuve, who directed Seydoux in Dune: Part Two, will release the final installment of this epic science-fiction trilogy will be on December 16. After that, he'll be free to focus on his next major project: reviving the world’s most famous secret agent. It remains to be seen who he will choose to star opposite Robert Pattinson as his female companion—but we know that despite her fondness for the director, Seydoux will not return: Just last month, the French actress told People “I really loved being on this franchise, but now it’s ... done.”

#3505. Is GTA 6 Too Easy? Rockstar Weighs In

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level. Some are saying it's too easy. Rockstar boss Rob Nelson has now entered the conversation, telling Destructoid that Rockstar's data showed that GTA 4 was "a little too punishing in places" and GTA 5 was "perhaps too easy." So with GTA 6, the team trying to "land somewhere in the middle."

GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition. That said, players can adjust things like aiming controls, while players can unlock cheat codes to make the game easier or harder.

Design producer Scott Mitchell, meanwhile, said the fail states in GTA 6 were designed to feel "appropriate."

“We wanted to keep things open and not limit the players’ use of mechanics, such as stealth, but we did also want to make sure we retained the cinematic, high production value, explosive sequences that we’re known for, and people expect. It feels like we’ve managed to strike a good balance," he explained.

Also in the interview, Nelson said figuring out the difficulty level for GTA 6 is itself challenging because the designers themselves know enemy positions better than anyone after playing and testing the game so much.

"There’s a real process in unpicking some of that to create an experience most players will be able to enjoy, rather than endure," Nelson said. "The game is so big, and has such a wide range of content that we can really lean into that, making certain open-world content--compounds and fronts for example---more difficult, to give players seeking a challenge something to sink their teeth into as well.”

GTA 6 launched on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one.

Before Milo Manheim was actually cast as Flynn Rider in the live-action Tangled movie, there were rumors that he was auditioning for it, and he was a popular fancast. So, it wasn’t a huge shock when he landed the role. However, some people thought he knew he’d be playing Rapunzel's love interest long before it was confirmed. Due to that assumption, the actor has gotten flak for not admitting he had the part sooner. Now, he’s set the record straight.

The news that Manheim had been cast as Flynn broke in January of 2026. It’s easy to assume that the School Spirits actor was made aware of this news long before we knew it. And considering the hype surrounding this project and the potential for him to play Flynn, I see why some may have been annoyed that the news wasn’t shared sooner. However, according to him, he didn’t even know he had the part until a few minutes before it was announced, as he told EW:

It’s important that the world knows this. People think that I booked this, like, a long time ago, and I’ve been keeping it a secret. I found out ten minutes before the news was released that I’d be playing Flynn.

It’s not super uncommon for actors to find out they’ve booked parts right before it’s publicly confirmed. In fact, David Corenswet learned he was Superman about an hour before the world did, per People. Also, Robert Pattinson landed the part of Bond on a Friday, according to Jeff Bezos, and his casting was publicly announced three days later on Monday. Sometimes, actors even find out they’ve gotten a gig at the same time as the rest of us. That’s what happened to Tom Holland; he learned he’d be playing Spider-Man on Instagram.

So, to those who were giving Manheim flak for not confirming his casting earlier, calm down. He didn’t know. In fact, it’s normal for actors to find out they’ve gotten parts right before they’ve been announced. Plus, even if he did know, it’s not like that’s information he can share.

With all that said and done, now it’s time to get excited about the live-action adaptation of Tangled. Production on the upcoming Disney movie wrapped in October, which means Manheim has lived out his dream of signing “I Have A Dream,” and he’s gotten to put his smoulder to good use. I bet he had a great time doing it too, because this is how he described his reaction to learning that he’d be playing Flynn Rider:

My skin was tingling that day. I was just flooded with dopamine and love and everything. But I can’t wait. I’m gonna really honor this movie and this role. I love Tangled, so here we go, adventure of a lifetime.

I sincerely hope they’ve had the adventure of a lifetime filming this movie, and I hope everyone can now get very excited for the Zombies star. It’s clear he cares a lot about playing Flynn, and he’s as thrilled as the fans are about this adaptation.

So, if you were annoyed he didn’t tell us about this sooner, stop. He didn’t know until we did, essentially, and now he’s played the part. All that’s left for us to do is anticipate his version of Flynn.

Now, we’ll have to wait a bit to see that, though, as the live-action version of Tangled is set to premiere on March 31, 2028. In the meantime, you can stream the animated Tangled with a Disney+ subscription and picture Milo Manheim as the beloved Flynn Rider.
